초안산-2031668.name: Choansan Mountain
초안산-2031668.description: Choansan is a mountain spanning Wolgye-dong in Nowon-gu and Changdong in Dobong-gu. It looks like a small neighborhood hill from the outside, but inside, several trails wind through fairly dense woods. Local residents regularly hike here, and there's a range of things to do, including a pottery-making experience and a campsite. Scattered across the mountain are the tombs of Joseon-era nobles and eunuchs, so it doubles as a bit of a history lesson.

백련사-강북-309307.name: Baengnyeonsa Temple (Gangbuk)
백련사-강북-309307.description: Baengnyeonsa is a temple of the Korean Buddhist Taego Order, tucked into the Samgaksan section of Bukhansan in Suyu 4-dong, Gangbuk-gu. Many temples dot the folds of Bukhansan — some with long, storied histories, others surviving only as a name on an old site — yet each remains a lotus ground of the Buddha regardless of age. Along the trail from the April 19th National Cemetery up to Daedongmun Gate sits this modest hall, easy to walk past. Founded in 1930 by Lee Eun-sun out of deep devotion, it has since become a place of practice and teaching — quietly keeping the Buddha's lamp lit to this day.

상수동-카페거리-2500207.name: Sangsu-dong Cafe Street
상수동-카페거리-2500207.description: Scattered around Sangsu-dong in Mapo-gu are riverside cafes with Han River views, which is why locals also call this the Hangang Cafe Street. From here you can see Bamseom Island near Seogang Bridge, the 63 Building, and the National Assembly across the water. At night the bridges light up spectacularly and car lights along the riverside road paint the scene gold. It's a compact, charming stretch that's just as nice for a stroll, and a favorite date spot for couples who like watching the night view over the river with music playing.

백악마루-2993160.name: Baegangmaru (Bugaksan Peak)
백악마루-2993160.description: Baegangmaru is the name for the summit of Bugaksan. At 342m it isn't especially tall on paper, but it's the clear high point of the area, cradling Gyeongbokgung Palace and the former Blue House while opening up a sweeping view over central Seoul. When the Hanyangdoseong city wall was first built in 1396, its roughly 97 construction sections were each named after a character from the Thousand Character Classic — Baegangmaru, as the starting point of the wall, corresponds to the very first character, '天' (cheon). As the highest point on the wall, it offers a full view of Hanyangdoseong stretching across Baegaksan and Inwangsan, plus a one-by-one look at the Bukhansan peaks beyond — Jokdurbong, Hyangnobong, Bibong, Seunggabong, Munsubong, and Hyeongjebong.

세종대왕-동상-1364932.name: King Sejong the Great Statue
세종대왕-동상-1364932.description: In Gwanghwamun Square, in front of Gyeongbokgung Palace, stands a statue of King Sejong the Great — built to honor Korea's most revered king, the first to be enthroned and to pass away at Gyeongbokgung. The bronze statue is 6.2m tall and 4.3m wide, seated and facing south, about 250m behind the Admiral Yi Sun-sin statue. Rather than projecting royal severity, Sejong's expression is gentle: he holds a book in one hand while the other seems to reach out warmly to his people. In front of the statue are replicas of instruments developed under his reign — an armillary sphere, a rain gauge, and a sundial — with a Joseon-dynasty timeline inscribed along a water channel at the plaza's edge. Relief carvings on six pillars behind the statue depict his achievements, and an entrance beneath leads down to the King Sejong Story exhibition hall. Sejong (r. 1418–1450), the 4th king of Joseon, created Hangeul, cemented Confucian governance, and greatly advanced science and culture during his reign.

북악산-809190.name: Bugaksan Mountain
북악산-809190.description: Bugaksan is the tallest of the four mountains ringing central Seoul (with Namsan, Naksan, and Inwangsan) and the high point of Bukhansan's southern ridge — the old city wall of Seoul was built starting from this peak. Sections of the original wall survive along the ridgeline, and Changuimun Gate (also called Jahamun), one of Seoul's four minor gates, sits in the saddle between Bugaksan and Inwangsan, connecting easily to downtown. The Bugak Skyway, running from Changuimun to Arirang Pass near Jeongneung, links a pavilion and pool along a scenic route through dense forest with sweeping city views, and connects onward to the former Blue House and Samcheong Park. At 342m, with a sharp triangular peak that stands out from its surroundings, Bugaksan was declared an auspicious site by the monk Muhak when Joseon was founded, leading to Gyeongbokgung Palace being built at its foot in 1394; the presidential office Gyeongmudae later stood on the same grounds.

대모산도시자연공원-1602451.name: Daemosan Urban Nature Park
대모산도시자연공원-1602451.description: Daemosan, in Gangnam-gu, is a modest 293m mountain also once known as Guksubong. Its shape reminded people of an old woman, earning it the nickname Halmisan ('Grandmother Mountain'), until it was renamed Daemosan by royal decree after King Taejong's tomb, Heolleung, was built nearby. At its entrance is a nature-study garden planted with rare trees, popular with schoolchildren on field trips and neighborhood walkers alike. Trails include a ridge path and a gentler loop path close to nature, with a stone tower built up over 20 years and a lookout point among its landmarks. A low-incline accessible trail added in 2021 lets visitors with mobility needs, older adults, and pregnant women safely enjoy the forest path too.

독립선언문-배부-터-2783547.name: Site of the Distribution of the Declaration of Independence
독립선언문-배부-터-2783547.description: Just across the street from Unhyeongung Palace in Jongno-gu stands a small marker reading 'Site of the Distribution of the Declaration of Independence.' This is where independence activists reviewed and distributed copies of the Declaration during the March 1st Movement of 1919; a stone in front lists the names of the 33 national representatives and comfort-women victims, giving passersby pause. The declaration was printed nearby at Boseong Printing House, then stored in the yard of the then under-construction Cheondogyo Central Temple (right next to today's marker) before being distributed to religious and student leaders. Easy to walk past on an ordinary street corner, it's a quiet but meaningful place to reflect on the courage of spring 1919.

사직공원-서울-127942.name: Sajik Park (Seoul)
사직공원-서울-127942.description: Jongno-gu has three well-known parks — Tapgol, Sajik, and Samcheong. Sajik Park, covering 188,710㎡ on the southeastern foot of Inwangsan west of the Government Complex, is built around Sajikdan Altar (a historic site), the first altar King Taejo Yi Seong-gye built alongside Jongmyo Shrine in 1395. 'Sa' refers to the god of earth and 'jik' to the god of the five grains — rites here prayed for a good harvest. The park today has a children's playground, statues of scholar Yi I (Yulgok) and his mother Shin Saimdang, the Hwanghakjeong archery range, and a children's library, with the Dangun Shrine and Jongno Public Library nearby; a five-minute walk up the adjoining trail leads to the Inwangsan hiking path.

낙원동-아구찜-거리-699222.name: Nakwon-dong Agujjim (Braised Monkfish) Street
낙원동-아구찜-거리-699222.description: In 1972, Seoul's first restaurant serving agujjim (spicy braised monkfish) opened on this street in Nakwon-dong — back then, the dish was known only in far-off Masan, and not even nearby Incheon, Seoul's closest coast, cooked monkfish this way. The original restaurant put enormous care into the recipe, since monkfish turns mushy when simply boiled; after trials with drying it on mountainsides and beaches (which brought hygiene problems from flies), cooks eventually found that alternating between ice water and boiling water kept the flesh firm. Word spread that Seoul now had proper agujjim, and more restaurants opened along the street — over a dozen at its peak — through ups and downs over the decades. Today the street is home to everything from restaurants only a few years old to ones running for over 30 years, serving alongside each other.

은평한옥마을-2724392.name: Eunpyeong Hanok Village
은평한옥마을-2724392.description: Eunpyeong Hanok Village, in Jingwan-dong, is a modern hanok (traditional house) village built after Bukchon and Seochon, forming a historic-culture district alongside Bukhansan National Park and Jingwansa Temple. Plots here were sold to individuals for building hanok only, so each house's shape and wood tone varies by owner's taste, making it enjoyable simply to look around. Walking paths and cafes make it pleasant for an outing. Since it's a residential area, the interiors of most houses — aside from commercial spaces — are private and not open to visitors, though a few owners do allow interior viewing by request.

법룡사-2757155.name: Beopnyongsa Temple
법룡사-2757155.description: Beopnyongsa, in Suseo-dong, Gangnam-gu, is a modern two-basement, three-story building shaped like a boat (a reference to the Prajna Ferry that carries beings to enlightenment). It serves as an education center for Buddhist nuns and lay practitioners nationwide, teaching practice, outreach, and social welfare, and training specialists across fields connected to Buddhism. It runs day and evening beginner and basic courses for lay Buddhists, and its cultural center offers classes in temple cuisine, folk painting, line exercise, traditional needlework, embroidery, yoga, flower arranging, tea ceremony, and Buddhist painting.

자양동-양꼬치거리-중국음식문화거리-2401757.name: Jayang-dong Lamb Skewer Street (Chinese Food Culture Street)
자양동-양꼬치거리-중국음식문화거리-2401757.description: Out exit 5 of Konkuk Univ. Station (Lines 2 and 7), past Rodeo Street, and about 50m toward the Han River is the Chinese food-culture street known as 'Lamb Skewer Street' — sometimes called Seoul's 'New Chinatown.' Lined with lamb-skewer restaurants run by ethnic Korean-Chinese, the street has more Chinese-language signage than Korean, and its lamb skewer joints and fusion Chinese restaurants make it a great spot to taste a different side of Seoul's food scene.

역삼개나리공원-2752545.name: Yeoksam Gaenari (Forsythia) Park
역삼개나리공원-2752545.description: A small neighborhood park near Exit 3 of Yeoksam Station, with a children's playground, exercise equipment for all ages, and pavilions and benches for resting. It's popular with nearby office workers for a lunchtime stroll or break, and is designated a no-smoking, no-drinking park by the Gangnam-gu Health Center.

망원정-터-127307.name: Site of Mangwonjeong Pavilion
망원정-터-127307.description: A pavilion in Hapjeong-dong, restored in October 1989 and designated a Seoul monument. Prince Hyoryeong built a country house here in 1424 (Sejong's 6th year); the following year, Sejong visited to inspect farming in the western suburbs and, caught in a welcome rain, named the pavilion Huiujeong ('Pavilion of Timely Rain'). In 1484, Prince Wolsan rebuilt it more grandly and renamed it Mangwonjeong. Lost to the 1925 flood and later Han River development, it was rebuilt as part of a riverside heritage restoration project, completed in October 1989. The neighborhood Mangwon-dong takes its name from this pavilion.

양천나눔누리타운-2611669.name: Yangcheon Nanumnuri Town
양천나눔누리타운-2611669.description: Near Sinjeong Negeori Station (Line 2), this two-basement, five-story, 1,800㎡ community center houses the Haenuri Food Market on the 1st floor, which distributes donated daily necessities to low-income residents. The 2nd floor holds a volunteer center connecting volunteers with local needs; the 3rd floor has classrooms and workshops for hands-on career exploration; the 4th floor runs a career/vocational experience support center for teens; and the 5th floor has a roughly 100-seat hall used for talks and events, available to rent in coordination with the volunteer center.

영등포-신길동-홍어거리-749355.name: Yeongdeungpo Singil-dong Skate (Hongeo) Street
영등포-신길동-홍어거리-749355.description: A cluster of restaurants near Usin Elementary School's intersection in Singil 4-dong specializing in hongeo (fermented skate) — a dish then known mainly from far-off Masan. The first hongeo restaurant opened here in the early 1990s; as more followed, hongeo lovers built up loyal followings over dishes like hongeo hoe (raw), muchim (seasoned), jjim (steamed), and aetang (soup). Other restaurants nearby gradually switched over to hongeo as it caught on, and — after a rough patch when several closed — the street rebuilt itself into today's hongeo-focused strip.

백범광장-백범-김구선생-동상-129418.name: Baekbeom Square (Statue of Kim Gu)
백범광장-백범-김구선생-동상-129418.description: Baekbeom Square sits partway up Namsan Park in Hoehyeon-dong, Jung-gu. Inside is a statue of independence activist, educator, and statesman Kim Gu (pen name Baekbeom), erected in August 1969 to honor his lifelong fight for independence and a unified Korea. Discussion of the statue began just two months after his assassination, and the site chosen — Namsan Park — had been the location of the colonial-era Joseon Shrine. Funded by donations from Korea and abroad, sculptors Kim Gyeong-seung and Min Bok-jin cast the 10m statue; groundbreaking was in April 1969, with the unveiling on August 23, his birthday. A broad lawn stretches out in front, with a path continuing up Namsan; the park also holds an equestrian statue of General Kim Yu-sin and a statue of independence figure Yi Si-yeong.

연남동-공방거리-2500201.name: Yeonnam-dong Workshop Street
연남동-공방거리-2500201.description: An arts-and-culture pocket in Yeonnam-dong, Mapo-gu, that grew up naturally near the Yeonnam-dong stretch of Gyeongui Line Forest Park. Young local artists and craftspeople run workshops and curated shops here, blending art into everyday life. Wandering the alleys turns up small stationery and object shops, quirky interior stores, and workshops making and selling handmade accessories, ceramics, candles, and leather goods.

서울창포원-749216.name: Seoul Iris Garden
서울창포원-749216.description: A themed ecological park built around iris flowers — one of the world's 'four great flowers' — with 12 zones including an iris garden, wetland garden, flower garden, and medicinal-plant garden. The iris garden alone holds 300,000 plants across 130 varieties, blooming from May to June. The wetland garden has decks for viewing aquatic plants and wetland creatures, the flower garden blooms seasonally with daylilies and tulips, and the medicinal-plant garden displays 130,000 plants across 70 species. There's also a succession-observation garden and forest rest areas, serving as ecological education and leisure space for residents. It's 125m from Exit 2 of Dobongsan Station (Lines 1 and 7), between Dobongsan and Suraksan, along the Dobongsan Dulle-gil trail.

방화대교-250166.name: Banghwa Bridge
방화대교-250166.description: Built to help Incheon International Airport serve as a 21st-century Northeast Asian hub, Banghwa Bridge is 2.6km long — the longest road bridge over the Han River — and Korea's first long-span arch-truss bridge, prized for both engineering and looks. Its arches echo the soft curves of traditional temple and tiled-roof eaves, forming what feels like a third artificial peak alongside nearby Gaehwasan and Deogyangsan. The bridge's geometric shape recalls a giant aircraft about to take off, and at night its reflection shimmering on the Han River draws admiring looks; lights come on from sunset until around 10pm. The sunset framed by the bridge's arches is a particularly striking sight, and its outer-Seoul setting makes it a good spot for a relaxed bike ride or walk.

정선옹주-묘역-2591833.name: Tomb of Princess Jeongseon
정선옹주-묘역-2591833.description: In Gung-dong, Guro-gu, this is the burial ground of the Andong Kwon clan, into which Princess Jeongseon — 7th daughter of King Seonjo, Joseon's 14th king — married. She wed Kwon Dae-im of the powerful Andong Kwon family and lived around what is now Gung-dong 67, which took its name ('Palace-dong') from their grand tiled residence resembling a palace. The tomb site holds Kwon Dae-im's grave alongside several other Andong Kwon burials and is often cited by geomancers as an especially auspicious site. Next door, Gung-dong Eco Park has trails, a rest pavilion, and exercise equipment amid 25,000 planted trees and flowers, with around 100 koi swimming in its pond — worth combining with a visit to the tomb.

궁동저수지-생태공원-2591809.name: Gung-dong Reservoir Eco Park
궁동저수지-생태공원-2591809.description: Built to improve the once-neglected old Gung-dong Reservoir and give Guro-gu residents an eco-friendly place to relax, with trails, a traditional Korean pavilion, rest areas, and exercise facilities amid 25,000 planted trees and flowers. There are spaces for observing wildlife and a children's playground, and about 100 koi swim in the ecological pond — scenery rarely seen elsewhere in Seoul. The park changes with the seasons: azaleas in spring, lotus in summer, reeds in autumn, and a frozen reservoir in winter. It sits right next to the Tomb of Princess Jeongseon, worth visiting together.

대원군별장-석파정-1605948.name: Regent's Villa (Seokpajeong)
대원군별장-석파정-1605948.description: A late-Joseon country retreat built for the Heungseon Daewongun (regent and father of King Gojong), designated a Seoul Tangible Cultural Heritage. Tucked into the rocky folds of Inwangsan, the Daewongun named it Seokpajeong; it's also known as the Samgye-dong pavilion. Originally comprising seven main buildings plus a hexagonal pavilion and other structures, only four survive today — the main hall, guest hall, annex, and pavilion — known for their scenic setting and refined architecture. It's now run by the Seoul Museum, whose exhibitions of modern and contemporary art come with access to Seokpajeong's outdoor grounds included in the admission ticket.

서울-운현궁-127454.name: Unhyeongung Royal Residence, Seoul
서울-운현궁-127454.description: Unlike a full palace such as Gyeongbokgung, Unhyeongung in Unni-dong, Jongno-gu, was the residence of royal relatives — specifically, home to the Heungseon Daewongun's family, and the house where King Gojong was born and raised before taking the throne. Most of the pivotal events of late Joseon history trace back here, from major reform policies to the isolationist foreign policy of the era, giving the site outsized historical weight. Its main buildings are Noandang and Norakdang, completed in September 1864, and Irodang, added six years later; of the four gates that once stood, only one remains. Norakdang, the central building, hosted major family events, while Noandang served as the Daewongun's personal reception hall — a classic Korean tile-roofed house known for its finely detailed eaves.

호암산성-1116022.name: Hoamsanseong Fortress
호암산성-1116022.description: A Silla-era fortress on Gwanaksan from the Three Kingdoms period, which pairs well with a visit to nearby cultural sites like Hanudeul Well and stone dog statues, or a walk on the Gwanaksan Dulle-gil trail past the traditional temple Hoapsa. Hoamsanseong is a Unified Silla-period mountaintop fortress encircling the ridge, 1,250m around, with roughly 300m of wall still visible today. Hanudeul (also called Yongbo) is a 22m by 12m granite-lined pond near the summit, used historically for rain-prayer rituals and as a wartime water source; excavations found an earlier Three Kingdoms-era pond buried beneath it, with the current stonework dating to early Joseon. A dog-shaped stone statue found near the well is thought to be tied to a Joseon-era legend about warding off fires in Seoul.

존비코올터장군상-1836254.name: Statue of General John B. Coulter
존비코올터장군상-1836254.description: Facing the statue of General Eulji Mundeok near the back gate of Seoul Children's Grand Park is this statue of General John B. Coulter, erected in Itaewon in October 1959 in gratitude for his role in rebuilding Korea after the Korean War, and relocated to the Grand Park in 1977. Coulter (1891–1983), deputy commander of the U.S. Eighth Army, commanded I Corps during the critical Battle of Pohang in 1950, helping halt the North Korean advance, and led supporting forces in the September counteroffensive into North Korea. After retiring in 1952, he served until 1958 as head of the UN Korean Reconstruction Agency, overseeing more than $200 million in reconstruction spending.

유관순동상-1828605.name: Statue of Yu Gwan-sun
유관순동상-1828605.description: Erected in Namsan Park in Jangchung-dong (near the entrance to Namsan Tunnel No. 2) to honor Yu Gwan-sun, who was arrested for leading the independence movement at Cheonan's Aunae Market and died in prison for the cause. A student at Ewha Haktang when the March 1st Movement broke out, Yu joined street demonstrations with classmates, then returned to her hometown of Byeongcheon, Cheonan, to organize protests when her school closed. On April 1, 1919, before a crowd of some 3,000 at Aunae Market, she distributed Korean flags she had prepared and led the march at the front, calling for independence. Japanese military police responded with bayonets and gunfire, killing 19 people on the spot — including her parents — and wounding around 30 more. Arrested as a ringleader, Yu was imprisoned at Seodaemun Prison, where she continued shouting for independence even behind bars; she died there from torture in October 1920, at just 18.

극락사-서울-1606052.name: Geungnaksa Temple (Seoul)
극락사-서울-1606052.description: Built on April 10, 1968, on a site King Taejo Yi Seong-gye once named 'Jeolgol.' Though the current building dates to 1968, it stands on a historic Joseon-era temple site and preserves traditional Buddhist architectural style, offering a quiet place to find peace of mind. The temple's grounds have a pretty garden and various Buddhist artifacts on display, and it draws many visitors seeking a moment of calm.

성덕사-1606096.name: Seongdeoksa Temple
성덕사-1606096.description: Tucked into a residential alley on the slopes of Bonghwasan in Sangbong-dong, Jungnang-gu, Seongdeoksa was founded in 1957 and includes a main hall, bell pavilion, and shrine halls to the Seven Stars, the Mountain Spirit, and Maitreya. Local legend holds the site was once considered ominous, until a visiting monk advised villagers to make an offering of red-bean porridge each Aedongji (early winter solstice) to settle old grudges tied to the land. A widow with four children kept up the ritual for years, and her children alone stayed healthy through a later village epidemic; she asked her descendants to continue it after her death. After liberation in 1945, construction here was oddly plagued by accidents until the temple itself was completed, after which such mishaps stopped — longtime locals say Seongdeoksa now performs the offering on the village's behalf.

봉화산근린공원-1115299.name: Bonghwasan Neighborhood Park
봉화산근린공원-1115299.description: This park has a brick-paved entrance plaza, a children's playground, a traditional-games area, a residents' fitness area, an outdoor stage, and rest areas. A 630m loop trail circles the park for jogging and walking, and there's a lawn plus an accessible fitness area near the summit. An artificial waterfall near the district office offers a rest spot for visitors, and an adjoining event plaza hosts the district's outdoor cultural performances. A 20–30 minute walk up the trail behind the park reaches the summit of Bonghwasan.

율곡로-250134.name: Yulgok-ro Road
율곡로-250134.description: A road framed by old palace walls and street trees. Changgyeonggung Palace and Jongmyo Shrine were originally connected, but in 1931 Japan's colonial government cut a road between them as part of its cultural-erasure policy — that road became Yulgok-ro. Despite its painful history, the street today has a quietly atmospheric feel, its weathered stone walls lined with trees. It takes its name from the pen name of Joseon scholar Yi I (Yulgok), who once lived in Gwanhun-dong, along the road's path. A major 30m-wide, 3km east–west artery running from Dongsipjagak past Ihwa-dong to Dongdaemun, it's known for its handsome streetscape.

반공순국용사-위령탑-1828631.name: Anti-Communist War Memorial Tower
반공순국용사-위령탑-1828631.description: A roughly 15m tower built to honor patriots who died fighting for the country. Following liberation in 1945 and again after North Korea's invasion in June 1950, members of patriotic groups along with police, firefighters, students, and other citizens gave their lives in defense of the nation. The memorial stands along Nodeul-gil beside the Yeouido side channel of the Han River, near Singil Station, and hosts a memorial service each June honoring their sacrifice.

용두동-쭈꾸미골목-2721231.name: Yongdu-dong Webfoot Octopus Alley
용두동-쭈꾸미골목-2721231.description: A street near Exit 6 of Jegi-dong Station (Line 1) specializing in jjukkumi (webfoot octopus), with restaurants dating back to the early 1990s. The signature dish is jjukkumi stir-fried on a hot iron plate with spicy seasoning. A golden octopus figure marks the entrance to the alley, which is lined with jjukkumi restaurants, many with loyal longtime regulars — part of the fun is picking whichever spot catches your eye.

천호자전거거리-2741610.name: Cheonho Bicycle Street
천호자전거거리-2741610.description: Along Cheonjung-ro on the way to the Han River, this street clustered with bike shops has long been a favorite destination for cycling enthusiasts and one of Gangdong-gu's signature themed streets. Beyond selling bikes, the shops here carry accessories, gear, and cycling apparel. Look for the whimsical sculpture 'Person on a Bicycle' and playful murals along the street, plus dedicated bike lanes that make it easy to ride.

봉화산-서울-1115042.name: Bonghwasan Mountain (Seoul)
봉화산-서울-1115042.description: Bonghwasan sits on Seoul's northeastern edge, touching Sangbong-dong, Junghwa-dong, Muk-dong, and Sinnae-dong in Jungnang-gu — an isolated hill rising just 160.1m from the surrounding plain, with wide-open views: Bulamsan and Dobongsan to the north, and Namsan and beyond to the south with no tall peaks in the way. Also known as 'Bongujae,' the area was transferred from Gyeonggi-do to Seoul in 1963. It once held a beacon-fire station relaying signals toward Namsan — restored in 1994. Slightly south of the summit stands a mountain-spirit shrine where villagers held communal rites as far back as roughly 400 years ago; the original shrine burned down in 1992 and was rebuilt in brick and concrete.

원당샘공원-2675091.name: Wondangsaem Park
원당샘공원-2675091.description: A park in Banghak-dong, Dobong-gu, tied to the roughly 600-year history of Wondang village, settled by the Papyeong Yun clan. Its centerpiece, Wondangsaem spring, takes its name from the village and supplied drinking water for centuries; it's now fed by groundwater and restored as a traditional pond so it never runs dry. The pond and its adjoining Samojeong pavilion make for a quietly pleasant stroll, shaded by around 13,000 trees planted during the restoration. In autumn, a Seoul-designated monument — a gingko tree over 800 years old — turns gold within the park, with a deck path around it for a closer look.

내원사-서울-298341.name: Naewonsa Temple (Seoul)
내원사-서울-298341.description: Set on the slopes of Samgaksan, about 1km up the Jeongneung valley with a view toward distant Mokmyeoksan. Its exact founding date and founder are unknown, but the site clearly carries some age. The clearest historical evidence comes from a 19th-century map and a woodblock kept at the temple, confirming it was still active in the early 1800s. Quite how or why it later vanished from the historical record is a mystery — even now, moss grows undisturbed on the old stone wall beneath the bell pavilion, and spring water still trickles quietly from the rocks.

달마사-서울-299978.name: Dalmasa Temple (Seoul)
달마사-서울-299978.description: A small temple halfway up Seodalsan, overlooking the Han River and Namsan across the water — by day watching the river flow by, by night the small lights of Namsan. Known as a serene training ground where mountain and city meet, it's a traditional urban temple offering a way to settle a mind worn down by the fast pace of the city. Morning prayers at dawn connect the temple with its neighbors, and it remains a quiet green pocket overlooking the Han River, a space the local community has made its own.

정암사-750927.name: Jeongamsa Temple
정암사-750927.description: A Taego Order temple on Bulamsan, on the border between Nowon-gu and Byeollae-myeon in Namyangju, Gyeonggi-do. Unlike most temples, it has no ilju-mun (one-pillar gate). Facing the main hall, Bulamsan rises on the left and Dobongsan's Jaunbong peak on the right, with views over Nowon-gu's streets to the front. The Yongwangdang shrine, dedicated to the dragon god of rain and water, houses an image of the Medicine Buddha and a spring for drinking water; up the mountain path behind the main hall, a rounded stone grotto holds shrines to the mountain spirit and Avalokiteshvara. Sitting right on a Bulamsan hiking trail, it's an easy stop mid-hike.

윌리엄해밀턴쇼-동상-1829586.name: Statue of William Hamilton Shaw
윌리엄해밀턴쇼-동상-1829586.description: This site tells the story of William Hamilton Shaw, born in Pyongyang to American missionary William Earl Shaw and raised alongside Korean friends, who gave his life for the country he loved. While pursuing a doctorate at Harvard to prepare for missionary work in Korea, he heard news of the outbreak of the Korean War and volunteered as a U.S. Navy officer. As an intelligence officer during the Incheon Landing, he contributed to the operation's success, and while leading forces advancing to retake Seoul, he was killed on September 22, 1950, in Nogbeon-dong, Eunpyeong-gu, at age 28. He was posthumously awarded Korea's Order of Military Merit and the U.S. Silver Star; in 2023, along with his missionary father, he was named one of the '10 Heroes of the Korean War' by Korea and the U.S.

무수골계곡-2759649.name: Musugol Valley
무수골계곡-2759649.description: Dobongsan, Seoul's northernmost mountain bordering Uijeongbu, Gyeonggi-do, rises to peaks of 740m and 683m, with several valleys beneath them. A long valley stretching down from near the summit toward the village below is known as Dobong Valley, or Musugol Valley — full of rocks and streams, and a popular escape from summer heat for hikers seeking mountains and water. Since it lies within Bukhansan National Park, access is only permitted during limited periods, and camping, cooking, smoking, pets, and noise-making are restricted or banned.

미타사-성북-309299.name: Mitasa Temple (Seongbuk)
미타사-성북-309299.description: Separated only by a wall from Bomunsa, Mitasa — better known as 'Tapgol Seungbang' — has long housed Buddhist nuns. Tradition holds it was founded in 950 by State Preceptor Hyego. In 1047, a stone pagoda was added, and the temple became known as Tapgol Seungbang ('pagoda nunnery'); that pagoda still stands on a rise behind the main hall. The temple was rebuilt in 1131, and again in the Joseon dynasty by Queen Dowager Songssi, widow of King Danjong. Its old six-tier stone pagoda is notable for having its upper and lower halves date to different periods, with the lower three tiers believed to date to Goryeo.

경국사-서울-294505.name: Gyeongguksa Temple (Seoul)
경국사-서울-294505.description: Founded in 1325 by Master Jajeongyulsa, originally named Cheongamsa for its location beneath Samgaksan's Cheongbong peak. In 1349, State Preceptor Taego Bou traveled to China, received dharma transmission, and returned to become royal preceptor under King Gongmin's invitation, receiving a golden kasaya robe here. In 1545, under King Myeongjong, Queen Dowager Munjeong sponsored Buddhist rites and renamed it Gyeongguksa ('temple of national blessing'). Former president Syngman Rhee is said to have visited together with then-U.S. Vice President Nixon, moved by the character of resident monk Bogyeong. From 1977 to 1985, the temple was transformed into its present form, and in 2005 a memorial stupa was raised here for Master Jaun, who devoted himself to reviving the precepts tradition in Korean Buddhism.

절두산-순교성지-126528.name: Jeoldusan Martyrs' Shrine
절두산-순교성지-126528.description: Jeoldusan was originally called Jamdubong for its resemblance to a silkworm's head. In February 1866, French warships sailed up the Han River over the persecution of Catholics; the enraged Heungseon Daewongun had large numbers of Catholics beheaded here in response, giving the site its later name, Jeoldusan ('Beheading Mountain'). Marking the 100th anniversary of the 1866 persecution's martyrdoms, the Korean Catholic Church opened a martyrs' memorial hall here in 1967. The shrine grounds today include a historical archive and relics hall, a chamber holding the remains of 28 canonized saints, a pilgrimage chapel, an education center, and outdoor exhibits — a deeply meaningful site where the spirit of Korea's early Catholic martyrs still lives on.

난지한강공원-127859.name: Nanji Hangang Park
난지한강공원-127859.description: Located between Hongjecheon Bridge and Nanjicheon Bridge, Nanji Hangang Park was redeveloped under the Han River Renaissance project, with new bridges improving access to Noeul Park, Haneul Park, and Peace Park. The Mirror Fountain near the Peace Park connector is the park's landmark, putting on a colorful lit water show whenever it runs. A riverside water-play area, open in summer with a max depth of 80cm, is popular with families with young children, and a pedestrian bridge over the wetland garden lets visitors observe native plants and wildlife up close. Nanji Camping Ground nearby is popular for barbecues and overnight stays, and the park's bike path connects east to Ttukseom Park and west to Goyang, Noeul Park, and Haneul Park.

송암사-750901.name: Songamsa Temple
송암사-750901.description: A Taego Order temple on Suraksan, with a main hall flanked by a stone Buddha and a Budae Hwasang (Hotei) statue, a stone pagoda in front, and a Buddha image carved into the rock face behind. Along with Doansa and Suamsa, it's one of several temples that can be visited along the Suraksan hiking trail.

아현동-전골목-749280.name: Ahyeon-dong Jeon (Savory Pancake) Alley
아현동-전골목-749280.description: Not as old as its market setting suggests — the oldest of the restaurants still open here dates only to the early 1990s. Short history aside, this alley of savory Korean pancakes (jeon) brings a lively energy to the traditional market scene and has become a cherished spot. Prices are low too — split an assorted jeon platter and a bowl of makgeolli between two, and you'll leave full and happy. A place to revisit old market memories, it quietly holds the everyday history of the working people who've made their living here.

학도암-서울-485684.name: Hakdoam Hermitage (Seoul)
학도암-서울-485684.description: Hakdoam's signature feature is a 13.4m rock-carved seated Avalokiteshvara (Guanyin) on a large cliff face behind the hermitage, commissioned in 1870 (King Gojong's 7th year) by Empress Myeongseong. The compassionate bodhisattva watches over all beings with a gentle smile, making it a landmark not just for the hermitage but for all of Nowon-gu. Cliff-carved Buddhas survive across the country, but ones depicting Avalokiteshvara are rare, and this one — among the largest and best-preserved — is considered an important cultural asset. Set amid scenery beautiful enough that cranes are said to have come to play here, Hakdoam remains a treasured place of worship beneath the country's largest rock-carved Avalokiteshvara.

락고재-컬쳐-라운지-애가헌-2992824.name: Rakgojae Culture Lounge Aegaheon
락고재-컬쳐-라운지-애가헌-2992824.description: Rakgojae Culture Lounge — its name meaning 'house of a beloved family' — is a Korean-culture experience space built with the hope that guests would enjoy traditional Korean culture in a home filled with love and happiness. Named an Excellent Hanok by Seoul in 2019, it reinterprets the Joseon-era sarangbang (men's reception room) as a space to enjoy Korean food culture and antiques. Reservation-only programs include Korean tea class, traditional liquor tasting, Korean cooking class, gayageum performance, and art programs. The space can also be rented for small weddings, first-birthday photoshoots, corporate events, and performances.

리얼월드-성수-2850356.name: RealWorld Seongsu
리얼월드-성수-2850356.description: RealWorld Seongsu, in Seongdong-gu, is a new-concept entertainment space blending play and culture in the city. Set in a mystery-hotel-themed space, visitors wander through immersive rooms combining a cafe with interactive escape-room-style games, becoming the protagonist of the story themselves. The ground-floor shop serves drinks and sells the interactive games, plus a photo zone for keepsake shots.

살곶이체육공원-753994.name: Salgoji Sports Park
살곶이체육공원-753994.description: Salgoji Sports Park sits near where Cheonggyecheon Stream meets Jungnangcheon, visible looking down from Hanyang University. It has multi-purpose sports facilities including an inline-skating rink, soccer field, basketball court, and badminton courts, with separate bike and pedestrian paths around the park. Walking races and short marathons are held here throughout the year, and it's a favorite with cyclists; a free water-play area runs in summer. The name Salgoji comes from a historical episode involving Joseon founder Yi Seong-gye and his son Yi Bang-won.

신기한놀이터-떼굴떼굴-2783484.name: Ttegul-ttegul Wonder Playground
신기한놀이터-떼굴떼굴-2783484.description: Set in an open-air space at the foot of a hill in a residential neighborhood, this natural sand playground lets children play safely and joyfully. Opened in November 2019 by Seodaemun-gu with the goal of building the playground children actually dream of, it has three sand play areas, foot-washing stations, drinking fountains, and public restrooms. The sand — East Coast beach sand suited for tactile play — is layered over 50cm deep across three circular play zones, and wooden play equipment, natural-wood boardwalks, and ochre-clay paving all use natural materials, working with the existing terrain to set it apart from typical playgrounds. A long slide and zip line draw curious kids, and children's bicycles and sand toys can be borrowed from the management office.

당고개순교성지-126803.name: Danggogae Martyrs' Shrine
당고개순교성지-126803.description: Just a five-minute walk from the Yongsan Electronics Market, on a small hill, is Danggogae Martyrs' Shrine — a site that produced 9 canonized saints and one beatified martyr. Here, at the tail end of the 1839 Gihae Persecution, ten Catholic men and women were martyred; they were originally to be executed at Seosomun, but were moved here after Seosomun merchants asked for the execution site to be relocated so as not to disrupt the Lunar New Year market. The shrine is built around the theme 'the pain of the wild rose thorn, the fragrance of the plum blossom' — persecution's suffering as the thorn, God's grace as the fragrance — and its 14 Stations of the Cross follow beatified martyr Maria Lee Seong-nye's path in imitation of Christ's, blending suffering with the glory of martyrdom. Its poignant history and sweeping view over Seoul draw a steady stream of pilgrims. It's close to Saenamteo Church and Yongsan Family Park, and a 15-minute walk from Exit 5 of Hyochang Park Station (Line 6).

해방촌마을-2761544.name: Haebangchon Village
해방촌마을-2761544.description: Haebangchon ('Liberation Village') got its name after Korea's 1945 liberation, when returning overseas Koreans, displaced people, and war refugees settled on this hillside below Namsan. Straddling Yongsan-dong 1-ga and 2-ga around Namsan, it's one of Seoul's classic hillside 'moon villages'; though designated for redevelopment in 1979, it kept its narrow alleys and steep lanes. A 2021 urban-regeneration project by Yongsan-gu improved the area for visitors exploring it by theme, adding a sloped elevator at the neighborhood's famous '108 Stairs.' Having appeared as a filming location in several dramas, it draws a steady stream of visitors.

파크하비오-워터킹덤-스파-2606150.name: Park Habio Water Kingdom & Spa
파크하비오-워터킹덤-스파-2606150.description: Water Kingdom is an indoor water park in Munjeong-dong, Songpa-gu, right in the city so there's no need to travel far, and open year-round regardless of weather. It has a wave pool, Korea's first 370m indoor 'Torrent River,' and a range of slides and tube, ball, body, and racing rides, plus jjimjilbang (sauna) and spa facilities for relaxing afterward.

옥천암-서울-337557.name: Okcheonam Hermitage (Seoul)
옥천암-서울-337557.description: 'Okcheon' means a spring of especially clear water — records say the spring here was believed to have healing properties, drawing the ill. The hermitage's Bodogak pavilion houses a rock-carved seated bodhisattva, also known as the Rock-Carved White Buddha or the Sea-and-Water Avalokiteshvara ('Bodo,' referring to Avalokiteshvara's vow to save all beings, is the more historically accurate name). Carved in the Goryeo-dynasty rock-relief style, the site likely developed under the influence of major nearby temples active since the Silla period. Legend holds that Joseon founder Yi Seong-gye prayed here when choosing Hanyang as his capital, that General Gwon Yul fought a battle here during the Japanese invasions, and that the wife of the Heungseon Daewongun prayed here for her son, the future King Gojong.

키즈오토파크-753850.name: Kids Auto Park
키즈오토파크-753850.description: Kids Auto Park, tucked behind the Imagination Land building in Seoul Children's Grand Park, is a traffic-safety experience center for children. It was jointly founded by an NGO (Korea Living Safety Federation), a company (Hyundai Motor Group), and the city government to teach children traffic safety in a fun, hands-on way. Spread over 3,000㎡ with driving courses and traffic signals, it lets kids actually drive small cars while learning traffic rules, alongside virtual driving simulators, pedestrian and driving training grounds, a traffic-safety 'license test' course, and more. Vehicles modeled on older Hyundai cars are used for safe, comfortable driving. Advance booking online is required. Children in grades 1–4 who complete the program can take a written, walking, and driving test to earn a children's traffic safety 'license.'

신사동-가로수길-987720.name: Sinsa-dong Garosugil
신사동-가로수길-987720.description: Garosugil ('tree-lined street'), in Sinsa-dong, Gangnam-gu, is one of the district's signature commercial strips, running from the intersection in front of Hyundai High School to Dosan-daero near Sinsa Station. Lined with charming cafes, restaurants, and designer clothing boutiques, it has an unmistakably international feel. Once known for its galleries and film-company offices, the street has since reshaped itself around fashion — home now to luxury brands, independent designers, and beauty labels alike, plus frequent fashion and beauty pop-up stores that keep the crowds coming.

동대문역사문화공원-1906334.name: Dongdaemun History & Culture Park
동대문역사문화공원-1906334.description: Built on the site of the old Dongdaemun Stadium in Jung-gu, this park doubles as a themed showcase of Seoul's history and culture and a venue for contemporary exhibitions, events, and public rest space. Demolition and park construction in 2008 uncovered part of the Hanyangdoseong city wall (including the Igansumun water gate and defensive bastions), the sites of the Hadogam and Hullyeondogam military offices, remains of 44 structures, and roughly 1,000 artifacts including Joseon-era white porcelain and buncheong ware, now preserved and displayed throughout the park. Near the entrance, the Dongdaemun Stadium Memorial Hall exhibits sports memorabilia, historical match records, and a model of the old stadium. It's 26m from Exit 1 of Dongdaemun History & Culture Park Station (Lines 2, 4, 5), a 10-minute walk from both Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP) and the Sindang-dong tteokbokki street.

충무로-인쇄골목-2865186.name: Chungmuro Printing Alley
충무로-인쇄골목-2865186.description: Chungmuro and adjoining Euljiro make up Seoul's historic printing district in Jung-gu — a dense cluster of printing businesses covering everything from commercial and digital printing to plate-making, with decades of history behind them. Chungmuro leans toward commercial and digital printing with modern equipment keeping pace with the fast-changing industry, while Euljiro is the traditional heart of the trade, home to plate-making and machine shops with old-school analog printing know-how. The two districts, a 10-minute walk apart, work together as an interlocking business ecosystem — a rare pocket where craft tradition and modern technology coexist.

본원정사-서울-316294.name: Bonwonjeongsa Temple (Seoul)
본원정사-서울-316294.description: Bonwonjeongsa, on Samgaksan in Suyu-dong, Gangbuk-gu, belongs to the Daegakhoe order of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism. It houses a wooden seated statue of Ksitigarbha (the bodhisattva who vows to save beings even in hell), said to have been moved here after a fire at Taegosa during the Korean War. In the early 1980s, the temple's then-abbot, Ven. Wonseong, was so moved by this statue that they took a vow to follow Ksitigarbha's original vow and renamed the temple Bonwonjeongsa ('temple of the original vow'). Since then, it has developed into a place for healing body and mind, remaining an always-open temple where Seoul residents and Buddhists alike can rest a busy mind and pray.

문래예술공장-2650230.name: Mullae Art Factory
문래예술공장-2650230.description: Mullae Art Factory, opened January 28, 2010, is a city-run creative-support center for artists working in and around the grassroots artist enclave of Mullae Changjakchon. Built anew inside a former steel-supply building on Mullae-dong's old machine-shop street, it offers shared studios, a multi-purpose performance hall, a recording studio, and seminar rooms supporting creation and public presentation. It functions as an open platform for boundary-crossing contemporary experimental art.

한국유림독립운동파리장서비-1836287.name: Monument to the Korean Confucian Scholars' Petition to Paris
한국유림독립운동파리장서비-1836287.description: This monument in Jangchungdan Park, Jung-gu, commemorates a letter Korean Confucian scholars submitted to the 1919 Paris Peace Conference appealing for Korean independence following the outbreak of the March 1st Movement. Known as the 'Paris Petition,' it exposed Japan's usurpation of Korean sovereignty, argued the illegitimacy of colonial rule and the legitimacy of Korean independence, and demonstrated to the world that the desire for independence spanned every class and group in Korean society. Signed by 137 Confucian scholars including Gwak Jong-seok and Kim Bok-han, the letter was carried to Shanghai by Kim Chang-suk and submitted to the peace conference through Kim Gyu-sik, and also distributed to foreign delegations, legations, and Confucian academies across the country. Japan responded by arresting and imprisoning participating scholars, which pushed the Confucian community to carry its late-Joseon tradition of national salvation into the independence movement. Since this first monument was erected in Jangchungdan Park, others have followed in Geochang (1977), Daegu (1997), Jeongeup (2008), and Bonghwa (2014).

무궁화동산-1603543.name: Mugunghwa (Hibiscus) Garden
무궁화동산-1603543.description: Built on the former site of a Central Intelligence Agency safe house in Gungjeong-dong, this citizens' rest park was once off-limits as part of the Blue House compound, opening to the public as a park after the road in front of the Blue House was opened in 1993. Mugunghwa (Korea's national flower, the rose of Sharon) is planted in a taegeuk pattern, with a fountain at the center shaped like the Chinese character for 'well,' symbolizing Gungjeong-dong. Natural stone walls ring the site, and a 240m walking path is lined with flower beds holding 7,700 wildflowers from across the country and roughly 1,500 trees of 13 species including mugunghwa, pine, and zelkova. Benches dot the grounds, making it a favorite rest spot for nearby residents.

삼청공원-126488.name: Samcheong Park
삼청공원-126488.description: Samcheong Park, in Samcheong-dong, Jongno-gu, was designated Seoul's first official urban park in March 1940. Set in the city center near galleries and specialty restaurants, it's a beloved walking spot with a quiet trail and scenic surroundings — cherry blossoms in spring, vivid foliage in autumn draw steady crowds. It holds a memorial stone honoring the loyal Goryeo minister Jeong Mong-ju and his mother, and a mineral spring up the valley trail; a children's forest-experience area makes it good for family visits. A forest library and cafe inside the park let visitors enjoy coffee and a book, and along the trail are a barefoot reflexology path, exercise equipment, badminton and tennis courts, a children's playground, and a snack stand.

세종로공원-1604697.name: Sejongno Park
세종로공원-1604697.description: Sejongno Park is a green space along Sejongno, the central avenue running from Gyeongbokgung Palace through Gwanghwamun and Sejong Center to Cheonggyecheon and Seoul Plaza. Once an aging, closed-off lot with limited public use, it was reopened and linked with Gwanghwamun Square to create a new space for civic life. Shaded pavilions and wooden benches throughout offer nearby office workers a downtown break, and a fountain, outdoor circular stage, and various sculptures add to its clean, well-kept, restful atmosphere.

선바위-선암-2774283.name: Seonbawi Rock
선바위-선암-2774283.description: Regarded as a sacred object, this rock is said to resemble a Buddhist monk wearing jangsam robes — its billowing black robe and wide sleeves — earning it the name Seonbawi, from the Buddhist character for 'seon' (meditation). Legend holds that when Joseon founder Yi Seong-gye was building Hanyang's city walls, the scholar-official Jeong Do-jeon and royal advisor Muhak Daesa clashed sharply over whether to place this rock inside or outside the wall: inside would favor Buddhism over Confucian scholar-officials, outside the reverse. Unable to decide, they woke the next morning to find snow that hadn't melted in one particular spot, which Taejo took as marking the wall's true line — placing the rock outside the city. A natural rock resembling a human figure, it isn't a direct object of worship, but has long been regarded with reverence as if it held Buddhist power.

서울-고려대학교-중앙도서관-250470.name: Korea University Central Library, Seoul
서울-고려대학교-중앙도서관-250470.description: Built to mark the 30th anniversary of Boseong College (Korea University's predecessor), this library was designed, like the main building, by Korean architect Park Dong-jin (1899–1982), reportedly modeled on Duke University's library in the U.S. — the alma mater of a professor at the time. Construction, begun in June 1935 and completed in September 1937, drew wide attention and support, funded without delay at a then-substantial cost of 220,000 won. Built of granite in Gothic style on the hill left of the main building, the five-story, L-shaped building centers on a corner tower, with one wing facing south alongside the tower and the other turning east. The main body is three stories, with a five-story Gothic-style tower of reinforced concrete faced in stone at the southwest corner. At completion, the ground floor held 32 faculty study rooms, the second floor a 250-seat reading room fitted with desk lamps and leather chairs, and the third floor housed 200,000 volumes, with folk artifacts and artwork displayed above. It's 300m from Exit 1 of Korea University Station (Line 6).

탈영역우정국-3082465.name: Post Territory Ujeongguk
탈영역우정국-3082465.description: In a residential neighborhood near Gwangheungchang Station (Line 6), Post Territory Ujeongguk is a long-term project by Reyeor Collective converting the former Changjeon-dong post office into a cultural space. The name combines 'ujeongguk' (the old word for post office), 'post' in its other sense of 'after,' and 'departing from' genre and boundary — together, 'the post office beyond boundaries.' Over its ten-year lease, the project explores boundary-free art through the interplay of physical space and content. The former postal workroom on the ground floor now hosts exhibitions, performances, and screenings, while the second floor (once staff housing) hosts smaller exhibitions, projects, and workshops. As a repurposed space, it still bears traces of its postal past — a large safe, an old incinerator — inside. Through video, painting, installation, performance, workshops, screenings, and talks, it consistently showcases experimental work by artists across visual art, performance, and experimental sound, bringing culture to nearby students and residents — and, unusually for a gallery, visitors can bring their pets.

금암문화공원-3082221.name: Geumam Culture Park
금암문화공원-3082221.description: Geumam Culture Park, in Guparbal, Jingwan-dong, Eunpyeong-gu, carries a piece of local history involving a grandfather and grandson from the late Joseon dynasty. The site once held Geumamcham, a relay station where messengers changed horses to carry military intelligence, and served as a resting point along the route kings took to visit royal tombs. King Jeongjo, Joseon's 22nd king, stopped to rest here on his way back from paying respects at his grandfather King Sukjong's tomb, and the resulting Geumamgijeokbi monument bears an inscription he composed recalling his grandfather King Yeongjo's benevolent rule. A 'hamabi' stone also stands here, inscribed with an order that everyone passing, in Joseon times, had to dismount from their horse. The park's children's playground uses LED lighting, multimedia, and sensors to make play and learning engaging, and there's a sand play area with an adjoining faucet for washing up. Across from the children's playground, adult exercise equipment lets grown-ups work out alongside their kids — some machines even light up when used, adding extra fun to evening workouts.

관악산자연공원-3081140.name: Gwanaksan Nature Park
관악산자연공원-3081140.description: Gwanaksan Nature Park, on Gwanaksan in Gwanak-gu, was designated an urban nature park in 1968 and remains one of Seoul's most-visited green spaces. It includes a lake park with pavilions and fountains for resting, a forest library stocked with children's and environmental books, an outdoor theater staging traditional Korean performances, a barrier-free forest trail, and an observatory. Notable planted species include hornbeam, wild chrysanthemum, and mountain forsythia, alongside natural monuments like Korean spindle trees and old-growth oak.

홍제천인공폭포-3452906.name: Hongjecheon Artificial Waterfall
홍제천인공폭포-3452906.description: Hongjecheon Artificial Waterfall is an oasis in the middle of the city. A dramatic 25m cascade offers a striking, cooling sight that helps wash away the fatigue of everyday life. Around the waterfall, walking paths, benches, and cafes make it easy to while away a relaxed afternoon.

양천해누리체육공원-2751345.name: Yangcheon Haenuri Sports Park
양천해누리체육공원-2751345.description: Haenuri Sports Park was Korea's first outdoor sports facility built on unused space inside a flood-retention basin. With an artificial-turf soccer field, futsal courts, jokgu (foot volleyball) courts, and outdoor basketball courts, it's widely used for club matches and events. Booking the soccer and futsal fields requires registering a team on the Yangcheon-gu Facilities Management Corporation website; slots open for first-come online booking each quarter.

개봉유수지-생태공원-2591792.name: Gaebong Retention Basin Eco Park
개봉유수지-생태공원-2591792.description: Gaebong Retention Basin Eco Park was built to restore a stable ecological base suited to a flood-retention basin's characteristics. Diverse habitat spaces linked to the surrounding residential area boost species diversity, connected into the city's wider ecological network via Mokgamcheon Stream. The park has an ecological wetland, a nature playground, a rose-and-hydrangea garden, a barefoot path, and a lawn plaza — a good outdoor classroom for children.

거리공원-2733966.name: Guro Street Park
거리공원-2733966.description: Guro Street Park, in Guro-gu, is a neighborhood park for local residents' leisure and rest. The service road running from Georipark's five-way intersection to Sindorim Station is named 'Georipark-gil' ('street park road') after the park it follows. It has walking paths and exercise equipment for a workout or stroll, plus children's play facilities that make it popular with families. A mix of trees and flowers gives it a changing seasonal look — cherry blossoms in spring, vivid foliage in autumn.

삼각어린이공원-2773287.name: Samgak Children's Park
삼각어린이공원-2773287.description: Samgak Children's Park, in Guro-dong, Guro-gu, was built to give neighborhood children a spacious, pleasant place to run and play safely. It's themed around an adventure through the solar system's planets, moons, and comets, with dynamic, imaginative play equipment kids love — mounded climbing structures, toddler combination play sets, net climbers, trampolines, hexagonal swings, rocking rides, and a zip line.

온수도시자연공원-잣절공원-2591824.name: Onsu Urban Nature Park (Jatjeol Park)
온수도시자연공원-잣절공원-2591824.description: Onsu Urban Nature Park straddles Yangcheon-gu and Guro-gu in southwestern Seoul, bordering Bucheon in Gyeonggi-do, with easy access via the Gyeongin national road, Nambusunhwan-ro, and the Gyeongin Expressway. Designated a park in 1971, it's a classic well-preserved natural park drawing roughly 180,000 visitors a year. Along the trails are mineral springs, badminton courts, a fitness area, benches, and exercise equipment like pull-up bars and waist-twisters, well liked by regular visitors. Jatjeol Park, within the larger park, has a pond and deck offering a cool spot in summer, and hosts an annual firefly-release event.

서울로-7017-2495561.name: Seoullo 7017
서울로-7017-2495561.description: The Seoul Station overpass, completed in the 1970s, faced demolition over structural safety concerns — but instead of tearing it down, the city repurposed it as 'Seoullo 7017' to bring new life to the area, reconnecting the once-divided streets around Seoul Station into 17 pedestrian paths. The name captures it all: a 1970s overpass reborn in 2017, transformed from a road for cars into 17 paths for people, standing 17m tall. True to its name, Seoullo 7017 links the once-fragmented city with 17 walking routes, breathing life back into the area. It has an information center, rest areas, a magnolia exhibit hall, cafes, an exhibition hall, a rose exhibit, and a garden classroom. Booking a walking-tour program in advance through the Visit Seoul website lets visitors explore Seoullo 7017 alongside nearby heritage sites like Culture Station Seoul 284, Namdaemun, and the Hanyangdoseong city wall with a professional city guide.

미타사-성동-309302.name: Mitasa Temple (Seongdong)
미타사-성동-309302.description: Mitasa, in Oksu-dong beneath Dalmajibong Park, is a temple directly affiliated with Jogyesa, the head temple of the Jogye Order. Sitting near the old river crossing 'Dumutgae,' it's also called Dumutgae Seungbang. Founded in 888 (Silla's Queen Jinseong's 2nd year) near today's Geumho-dong by a devout nun's vow, it was relocated to present-day Oksu-dong in 1115 by two nuns, who built the Geungnakjeon hall, enshrined an Amitabha Buddha, and received the temple's name from a state preceptor. Its Geungnakjeon and Gwaneumjeon halls were built through the devout patronage of a Joseon-era queen dowager; the Geungnakjeon's triad of Buddhas and six ritual paintings, the Gwaneumjeon's Thousand-Armed Avalokiteshvara painting, and a seven-story stone pagoda all embody the traditional beauty of Buddhist art. Over the centuries, many nuns gathered here and built their own hermitages within the grounds — today there are seven, making it a distinctive traditional temple complex in the heart of Seoul. In 1988, it built the Cheonbuljeon hall and Mita Kindergarten, now serving as a spiritual home for local residents and a childcare center for the neighborhood's children.

보성사터-605497.name: Site of Boseong Printing House
보성사터-605497.description: Boseong Printing House was formed in late 1910 by merging Changsinsa with the print shop of Boseong Academy, and operated under the Cheondogyo religious movement. It printed 20,000 copies of the Declaration of Independence for the March 1st Movement. Company president Lee Jong-il, together with factory supervisor Kim Heung-gyu and secretary-general Jang Hyo-geun, printed the declaration here on the night of February 27, 1919, carried the copies to his own home, and distributed them nationwide the next day, laying the groundwork for the independence movement. Housed in a two-story brick-and-tile building on the grounds of Jeondong Boseong School, the printing was carried out at the special order of Cheondogyo leader Son Byeong-hui (its owner), using a draft written by Choi Nam-seon and signed by the 33 national representatives — 35,000 copies were printed that night, narrowly escaping detection by Japanese police by disguising the print job as genealogy books. Japanese authorities shut the print shop down and burned it to the ground on the night of June 28, 1919, leaving only the site behind, in what is today the grounds of Jogyesa Temple in Jongno-gu; a memorial monument and statue stand in the small park across from Jogyesa's rear gate.

서울색공원-1369066.name: Seoul Color Park
서울색공원-1369066.description: Seoul Color Park (about 9,000㎡) occupies the space beneath Mapo Bridge between its piers and the riverbank, built around the theme of 'Seoul Color' — a city-wide palette developed to improve Seoul's visual environment and build a distinct urban identity, applied here to public space. It gives Han River visitors both a place to rest and a chance to experience everyday design. The park includes a Seoul-color sculpture evoking the river's waves, and benches and graphics using a barcode motif built from Seoul's 10 representative colors. Public facilities use muted roof-tile gray and stone-wall gray to blend into the streetscape, while more visible elements use vivid colors — dancheong red, ochre-wall yellow, Namsan green, and their related shades — systematically improving the city's visual character. The same Seoul Color palette also appears in installations at the Seoul Museum of Art and the Seoul Museum of History.

서울-구의정수장-제1-2공장-구의-아리수-정수센터-2452856.name: Guui Water Purification Plants No.1 & 2, Seoul (Guui Arisu Water Center)
서울-구의정수장-제1-2공장-구의-아리수-정수센터-2452856.description: The Guui Arisu Water Center traces the full history of Korea's water-treatment technology in one place. Plants No. 1 and 2, which produced tap water from 1941 to 2002, were designated a National Registered Cultural Heritage in 2007. The center has an exhibition hall detailing Arisu, Seoul's tap water brand, plus tours of the treatment process, and runs age-tailored heritage education programs for children, teens, and adults — young children learn how Han River water becomes tap water through hands-on water-environment activities, school groups explore when tap water production began and where their school's drinking water comes from, and adults can tour the historic Plant No. 1 and No. 2 facilities. Programs run twice on weekdays, at 10am and 2pm, bookable via Seoul's public-service reservation website or by phone.

신트리공원-서울-2611887.name: Sintri Park, Seoul
신트리공원-서울-2611887.description: Sintri Park is a signature neighborhood park in Yangcheon-gu, where everyday relaxation and nature coexist. A 2025 renovation — including a new indoor playground — reopened it as a welcoming space for anyone to relax, socialize, and connect with nature. It has a forest walking trail, shaded rest areas, an exercise zone, a lounge area, a forest playground, a rose garden, and an ochre-clay path. An agricultural classroom doubles as an urban-farming learning space where visitors tend and observe crops watered with reclaimed rainwater.

이태원-우사단길-2650771.name: Itaewon Usadan-gil
이태원-우사단길-2650771.description: Usadan-gil blends Korean everyday life with an international atmosphere. Restaurants from Pakistan, Turkey, Egypt, Lebanon, India, and beyond, Arabic-lettered signs, and passersby in hijabs and turbans give the street a distinctly foreign feel, while its close-knit alleys of older homes retain a genuinely Korean residential character. Since the early 2010s, young artists and entrepreneurs have moved in, filling the street with distinctive small spaces.

왜고개-2758125.name: Waegogae
왜고개-2758125.description: Waegogae takes its name from the 'waeseo,' a kiln workshop here that fired roof tiles and bricks — reportedly including the bricks used to build Seoul's Myeongdong Cathedral and Yakhyeon Cathedral in Jungnim-dong. This historic Catholic site was where saints martyred at Saenamteo and Seosomun during the 1866 Byeongin Persecution were buried. It's also where the body of Fr. Andrew Kim Dae-geon, Korea's first Catholic priest, martyred in the 1846 Byeongo Persecution, was interred before being later moved elsewhere.

여의도한강공원-멀티프라자-2760268.name: Yeouido Hangang Park Multi Plaza
여의도한강공원-멀티프라자-2760268.description: The Multi Plaza, a lawn square inside Yeouido Hangang Park, is one of Seoul's signature leisure spaces — a multi-purpose venue for culture and recreation set against the Han River's scenery. It hosts the Seoul Fireworks Festival and has previously hosted riverside concerts by the Seoul Philharmonic, with seasonal events and festivals offering visitors something special year-round. A quirky shade installation from a 2021 public-design project, 'Cloud Canopy,' makes round white 'clouds' appear to float over the green lawn, popular with picnickers for the shade it provides. Its convenient location and range of amenities make it one of the park's most-loved spots.

한복남-경복궁점-2390314.name: Hanbok Nam Gyeongbokgung Branch
한복남-경복궁점-2390314.description: Hanbok Nam is a cultural-entertainment company built around shared hanbok (Korean traditional dress) experiences, always working on new projects and products. Its Gyeongbokgung branch spans basement level to 3rd floor and stocks around 1,000 hanbok in a range of designs and sizes. It's linked with a professional studio offering paid hanbok portrait sessions and snap-photo packages, bookable through its website. 'The man who dresses you in hanbok' offers a fun window into a side of Korea many visitors haven't seen.

후암별채-2932122.name: Huam Byeolchae
후암별채-2932122.description: A private space reserved entirely for one person — a place to relax and enjoy the water alone. Unwind tired muscles with a half-body bath and a warm cup of tea. It operates by reservation only, as a single-occupancy space.

서빙고동-부군당-1603296.name: Seobinggo-dong Bugundang Shrine
서빙고동-부군당-1603296.description: Seobinggo-dong Bugundang is a shrine local villagers built during the Joseon dynasty to protect the village and ensure residents' well-being. 'Bugundang' is a name for this type of shrine used only in Seoul and its surrounding Gyeonggi area. This small tile-roofed shrine building not only illustrates late-Joseon shrine architecture but also reflects Seoul's tradition of village guardian-spirit worship; it preserves five wooden plaques — including one hung during renovations in 1635 (King Injo's 13th year) — and shamanic paintings. The paintings are said to depict King Taejo and his queen, and gods of childbirth, life, and farming, all regarded as guardian deities protecting the village.

후암거실-2767753.name: Huam Living Room
후암거실-2767753.description: Near Seoul Station, Huam Living Room is a cozy private space for watching movies on your own terms. With Namsan and N Seoul Tower in view and a full home-theater setup (4K-capable projector and 5.1-channel speakers), it's a shared living-room space for spending quality time with a partner or friends. The interior, styled with teal sofas and natural-wood furniture, has a sleek, eye-catching look. The 1st and 2nd floors house Cafe Huam Yeollip, serving simple drinks, desserts, and alcohol, where visitors can take in a night view of N Seoul Tower in a quiet, relaxed setting.

디키디키-2561208.name: DKDK (Design Kids Digital Kids)
디키디키-2561208.description: DKDK — short for 'Design Kids Digital Kids' — is a large-scale playground designed to nurture children's sensibility and creativity through design, letting even very young children naturally absorb a design mindset across culture, art, and industry. It offers a fresh, healthy play culture blending analog play with digital media in a 'digilog' concept. Packed with activities that build creativity and social skills, it's a special place that gives children a genuinely fun experience.

서리풀공원-2773409.name: Seoripul Park
서리풀공원-2773409.description: Seoripul Park, a favorite of Seorae Village residents, is a space for rest and wellness. Off-limits for decades while a military base occupied the site in the 1970s, it was developed into a park in 2019 following the base's 2015 relocation. Its trails run through the heart of Seocho-gu from Banpo-dong to Bangbae-dong via two routes — a quick path and a leisurely one. The roughly 4km trail continues to Montmartre Park, with the Nue Bridge and Seoripul Bridge stitching together sections otherwise cut off by roads, opening views north to the Han River and south to Umyeonsan.

양재근린공원-2773271.name: Yangjae Neighborhood Park
양재근린공원-2773271.description: Yangjae Neighborhood Park is a well-tended, forest-like park in the city that draws steady crowds. Sitting between Eonnam Middle/High School and Maeheon Elementary School, it serves as an after-school retreat for students and a sports facility for nearby residents alike. It has a playground, fountain, benches, and walking paths, plus a basketball court, playground, soccer field, and sports ground — the soccer field even hosts the Seoul Citizens' League (futsal). With cherry blossoms in spring and vivid foliage in autumn, it draws visitors year-round as an important pocket of nature in the heart of Seoul.

우면산자연생태공원-2757831.name: Umyeonsan Nature Ecology Park
우면산자연생태공원-2757831.description: Umyeonsan, at 293m, is an easily climbed mountain right in the city, spanning Umyeon-dong, Seocho-dong, and Yangjae-dong in Seocho-gu. Its name means 'sleeping cow mountain,' after its resemblance to a dozing cow's silhouette. A Bronze Age dolmen on its southern slope shows this area has been settled since ancient times. Designated and managed as one of Seoul's urban nature parks, Umyeonsan combines walking and hiking trails with mineral springs, Buddhist temples like Daeseongsa, historical sites including the tomb of Jeong Do-jeon and a shrine to Yi Jon-o, and the Seoul Arts Center, all woven together into a cozy retreat for city residents — more a place to enjoy nature as it is than a manicured educational trail.

여의천-2391348.name: Yeouicheon Stream
여의천-2391348.description: Yeouicheon rises on Cheonggyesan in Sinwon-dong, Seocho-gu, and flows into Yangjaecheon Stream, part of the Han River watershed and the first tributary of Yangjaecheon. Once called 'Yeomgokcheon,' it was also known locally as 'Yeonnaecheon' ('misty stream') for how often fog settled over it. It runs 4.85km with a 6.87km watercourse and a 12.98㎢ drainage basin. Yeouicheon is something of a hidden cherry-blossom spot — cherry trees along its banks turn a soft pink each spring, drawing photographers and strollers alike when they reach full bloom.

대성사-서울-300076.name: Daeseongsa Temple (Seoul)
대성사-서울-300076.description: According to tradition, the monk Marananta suffered from illness on his journey to Baekje but was cured after drinking water from Umyeonsan, and built the hermitage Daeseongchodang here in gratitude — the origin of today's Daeseongsa. Ven. Baek Yong-seong, one of the 33 national representatives of the March 1st Movement, later resided here, taking part as a Buddhist representative in the movement's broader push for independence. The temple today holds a wooden seated Buddha statue (a Seoul Tangible Cultural Heritage) made under Ven. Baek Yong-seong.

안양천제방벚꽃길-2774291.name: Anyangcheon Levee Cherry Blossom Path
안양천제방벚꽃길-2774291.description: Running along the Anyangcheon Stream levee from Yeongdeungpo-gu all the way to Gwangmyeong, this is Seoul's longest cherry blossom path. Each spring, the towering cherry trees lining the levee road make it one of the city's premier cherry-blossom destinations for a leisurely stroll. With apartment complexes lined up along the levee, locals use it year-round for exercise and walks; in cherry-blossom season it fills with people enjoying the blossoms alongside the flower beds, eco park, sports facilities, and rest areas built along the stream, as well as cyclists. Along the levee and streamside, seasonal themed gardens and photo spots have been added alongside ecological restoration work, giving visitors plenty to see and do.

오동근린공원-866393.name: Odong Neighborhood Park
오동근린공원-866393.description: Odong Neighborhood Park spans Gangbuk-gu and Seongbuk-gu — a large park covering Beon-dong, Mia-dong, and five other neighborhoods in Gangbuk-gu, plus Wolgok-dong in Seongbuk-gu. Well-forested, it has fitness facilities, a badminton court, a children's forest-experience area, a playground, and rest areas, serving as a place for rest and exercise for residents of the surrounding housing developments.

뚝섬한강공원-벽천마당-2756578.name: Ttukseom Hangang Park Byeokcheon Plaza
뚝섬한강공원-벽천마당-2756578.description: Ttukseom Hangang Park has a fountain where water jets rise straight from the ground, and Byeokcheon Plaza, a rock-climbing wall area. Along with the floating fountain at Yeouido Hangang Park and the Mirror Fountain at Nanji Hangang Park, it's one of Seoul's three great Han River fountain spots — the illuminated night fountain here is especially striking, its lights mingling with the glow of the Han River bridges and the Gangnam skyline. Sitting on the grass and watching windsurfers, water-skiers, and motorboats out on the river is a great way to shake off the fatigue of city life.

남산공원-서울-126485.name: Namsan Park (Seoul)
남산공원-서울-126485.description: Namsan Park, in the heart of Seoul, is a natural retreat that gives city residents fresh air, and a hub of leisure activity centered on N Seoul Tower and the Namsan cable car, alongside walking, exercise, and rest. Its official name is Namsan Urban Nature Park. Namsan, a symbol of Seoul at the city's center, was originally called Ingyeongsan; after Joseon founder Taejo moved the capital from Gaeseong to Seoul, the mountain to the south came to be called 'Namsan' ('south mountain'), and it also holds geomantic importance as Seoul's 'ansan' (facing mountain). An eight-year 'Restoring Namsan's True Form' project starting in 1991 relocated 89 unsightly structures and built an outdoor botanical garden, extensively restoring the surrounding Yejang-dong, Hoehyeon-dong, and Hannam-dong areas — turning the mountain into a hub for rest, clean air, and leisure. Along the path up to the N Seoul Tower observatory is Namsan's famous 'Locks of Love,' already covered with countless padlocks symbolizing lovers' devotion — reading the messages written on them is a small pleasure of the climb. Since May 1, 2005, private cars and taxis have been banned from Namsan Park; visitors reach N Seoul Tower via circular bus from Myeongdong, Chungmuro, or Dongguk Univ. Station, the cable car, or on foot.

남산-팔각정-1603336.name: Namsan Palgakjeong (Octagonal Pavilion)
남산-팔각정-1603336.description: Namsan Palgakjeong, alongside N Seoul Tower, is one of Namsan's signature landmarks. Standing at the summit, it commands a sweeping view of the city and a striking night skyline, drawing steady crowds of residents and tourists. It's reachable on foot, by the Namsan circular shuttle bus, or by cable car.

여계묘역-2591819.name: Tomb of the Hamyang Yeo Clan
여계묘역-2591819.description: This is the ancestral burial ground of the Hamyang Yeo clan, in Gocheok 2-dong, Guro-gu. The clan traces its founding ancestor to Yeo Eo-mae, a Hallim Academy scholar of Tang China who fled to Silla in 877 during the Huang Chao rebellion. The grounds hold the tomb of a court official who served as deputy and then vice minister of taxation under King Taejong in the early Joseon period, alongside that of his wife, of the Cheongsong Sim clan, arranged one above the other. The tomb was built in 1428 (King Sejong's 10th year); the wife was the granddaughter of a state councilor and daughter of a court judge. Covering 1,025㎡, the site has two burial mounds, one tombstone, two stone offering tables, and two pairs of civil- and military-official stone figures — of significant value for research into early-Joseon tomb style and stonework.

옛-용산신학교와-원효로-예수성심성당-127016.name: Former Yongsan Seminary and Wonhyoro Sacred Heart of Jesus Cathedral
옛-용산신학교와-원효로-예수성심성당-127016.description: Yongsan Seminary was built in 1892 and Wonhyoro Sacred Heart of Jesus Cathedral in 1902, both designed and overseen by the French priest Father Coste. Yongsan Seminary, a semi-basement, two-story brick building, was Korea's first seminary building. The seminary later moved to what is now Hyehwa-dong; this building served as a branch of Seoul St. Mary's Hospital before being taken over by the Sisters of the Sacred Heart in 1956, and while some sections have been added on, most of the original structure remains. Built into a hillside, Wonhyoro Cathedral is three stories on its south (downhill) side and two on the north, with its main entrance set off-center for an asymmetrical look. Inside, it's a simple hall with only an altar and pews, but its pointed-arch windows and small spires give it a simplified Gothic character. Stepping inside, visitors are struck by the central stained-glass window depicting the Sacred Heart's love spreading across the world — one of the required stops on any tour of Korean church art. Around a decade ago, the French stained-glass artist Brother Marco added subtle glasswork to the side walls and rear second floor, so the whole cathedral now shifts color hour by hour as sunlight moves across it. Above all, both buildings are registered Catholic pilgrimage sites: Fr. Andrew Kim Dae-geon's remains rested here for over 50 years, and the site once served as a junior seminary training priests, drawing many pilgrims every year.

윤동주-하숙집-터-2993372.name: Site of Yun Dong-ju's Boarding House
윤동주-하숙집-터-2993372.description: This is the site of the boarding house where the ill-fated genius poet Yun Dong-ju once lived. After enrolling at Yonhui College (now Yonsei University) in 1938, the poet moved through several lodgings before living at '9 Nusang-dong, Jongno-gu' from May to September 1941 — the home of novelist Kim Song, a writer Yun deeply admired. Though he stayed only about five months, it was here that he wrote ten of his finest poems, including 'Counting Stars at Night' and 'Self-Portrait,' making the site a meaningful destination that still draws a steady stream of visitors. The original tile-roofed hanok is gone, replaced today by a multi-unit house whose wall bears only a small sign reading 'Yun Dong-ju's Boarding House.' About 180m from the site lies Suseongdong Valley, the entrance to Inwangsan. Yun's friend and one-time roommate, later Seoul National University professor Jeong Byeong-uk, recalled: 'Before breakfast we'd walk up to the middle of Inwangsan behind the house, wash our faces somewhere in the valley, come back to clean the room, have breakfast, and go to school.' The place offers a small window into the private life of Korea's beloved national poet.

필운동-홍건익-가옥-2783558.name: Piraun-dong Hong Geon-ik House
필운동-홍건익-가옥-2783558.description: The Piraun-dong Hong Geon-ik House comprises five wood-and-tile buildings, an inner gate to the rear garden, and a circular stone well.
