Long said by oral tradition to have belonged to the statesman Yi Hang-bok (pen name Baeksa, 1556–1618), the house is now believed to have been newly built by Hong Geon-ik between 1934 and 1936, after demolishing an earlier house on the same lot. Before Hong built here, the roughly 467-pyeong site was home to Go Yeong-ju, a reform-minded interpreter-official, and later Sim Jae-hong, grandson of a minister of the Korean Empire who opposed the Eulsa Treaty to the end. The house is arranged across a narrow, gently sloped lot divided into terraced levels, with the main gate, gatehouse, servants' quarters, men's quarters and inner gate building, women's quarters, and a detached building laid out in sequence from front to back. (Source: Korea Heritage Service)

경희궁공원-1604824.name: Gyeonghuigung Park
경희궁공원-1604824.description: Gyeonghuigung Park is a handsome space where Seoul's history and nature come together, built around the Joseon-era Gyeonghuigung Palace, blending old-style architecture with a variety of plantings. Its walking paths and lawns let visitors take in the historic atmosphere of the former palace grounds while relaxing — a well-loved heritage-protected green space in the city.

홍지문-및-탕춘대성-129506.name: Hongjimun Gate and Tangchundaeseong Fortress
홍지문-및-탕춘대성-129506.description: Tangchundaeseong is a uniquely structured late-Joseon defensive wall connecting Hanyang's city wall to Bukhansanseong Fortress, built to close the blind spot in the terrain between the two. Roughly 4km around, it enclosed a military training ground and grain storehouses; built of evenly cut square stone blocks, its walls illustrate the fortress-building techniques of King Sukjong's reign. Hongjimun Gate has a three-bay, two-story gate tower with a hip roof above its arched opening, and the adjoining Ogansu-daemun water gate uses five arched openings as a water outlet. The fortress takes its name from Tangchundae, a pavilion built on the peak east of Segeomjeong during King Yeonsangun's reign for banquets; Hongjimun was also known as Hanbukmun. Flood in 1921 destroyed Hongjimun and the water gate; both were rebuilt along with Tangchundaeseong in 1977.

다락원체육공원-2764354.name: Darakwon Sports Park
다락원체육공원-2764354.description: Darakwon Sports Park, at the foot of Dobongsan in Seoul, is a comprehensive sports complex with tennis, badminton, and soccer facilities among others. Its tennis courts include 3 indoor courts plus outdoor courts; its badminton hall is a large indoor facility with 14 well-maintained wooden-floor courts; and its soccer field has night lighting for evening use. Ample parking and amenities make it convenient for visitors.

청룡사-서울-482153.name: Cheongnyongsa Temple (Seoul)
청룡사-서울-482153.description: Cheongnyongsa, in Sungin-dong, Jongno-gu, is a branch temple of Jogyesa, the head temple of the Jogye Order's direct-administration district. It was founded in 922 on the orders of Taejo Wang Geon of Goryeo, per the will of the monk Doseon. Its name, 'Blue Dragon Temple,' comes from its location on a ridge geomantically corresponding to Hanyang's 'outer blue dragon.' The nun Manseon carried out the temple's first major reconstruction in 1036 after it had fallen into disrepair, and it has since undergone ten rounds of rebuilding. It was renamed back to its original Cheongnyongsa in 1923, saw major reconstruction in the 1950s, and was rebuilt again in 1973, arriving at its present form.

구룡산-서울-2357761.name: Guryongsan Mountain (Seoul)
구룡산-서울-2357761.description: Guryongsan (306m) shares a ridge with Daemosan and sits across Yeomgok-dong in Seocho-gu and Gaepo-dong in Gangnam-gu. Neither tall nor rugged, it makes for an easy, unintimidating hike. Legend holds that a pregnant woman once saw ten dragons ascending to heaven and cried out in shock, causing one to fall to its death while the other nine made it to the sky — giving the mountain its name, 'nine dragons.' The dragon that fell is said to have become the water of Yangjaecheon Stream. The mountain's main peak, lower than its true summit, is called Guksubong ('nation-guarding peak'), named for a beacon-fire station that stood there from before the Joseon dynasty to defend the country; a rock cave here is said to have housed the beacon-fire guards.

서울-헌릉-태종-원경왕후-과-인릉-순조-순원황후-유네스코-세계유산-126.name: Heolleung (Tombs of King Taejong and Queen Wongyeong) and Illeung (Tombs of King Sunjo and Empress Sunwon), Seoul [UNESCO World Heritage]
서울-헌릉-태종-원경왕후-과-인릉-순조-순원황후-유네스코-세계유산-126.description: Heolleung is the tomb of Joseon's 3rd king, Taejong (r. 1400–1418), and Queen Wongyeong (1365–1420), in the 'twin tomb' style with two mounds side by side inside a single enclosure — facing the tomb, Taejong's mound is on the left (west) and Queen Wongyeong's on the right (east). Queen Wongyeong died first, in 1420; Taejong had his own burial plot prepared alongside hers at that time, and when he died two years later his tomb was built to the west of hers. Both mounds are ringed with stone guard-screens and balustrades, carved with the twelve zodiac guardian figures and ritual vajra emblems, and surrounded by civil- and military-official stone figures, stone horses, an incense table, a stone lantern, a spirit-repose stone, pillar stones, and stone sheep and tigers — twice as many as most royal tombs, following the precedent of the Goryeo tombs of King Gongmin and Princess Noguk. Illeung is the tomb of Joseon's 23rd king, Sunjo (r. 1800–1834), and Empress Sunwon (1789–1857), in the single-mound 'joint burial' style. Built first near Jangneung in Paju Gyoha after Sunjo's 1834 death, it was relocated to its present site in 1856 after being judged inauspicious by geomancers — a site that had originally held King Sejong's old tomb, whose unearthed stone furnishings, along with those of Queen Janggyeong's old tomb nearby, were refinished and reused here. Empress Sunwon was interred alongside him the following year.

서울-살곶이-다리-753989.name: Salgoji Bridge, Seoul
서울-살곶이-다리-753989.description: Construction of this bridge began in 1420 to accommodate the frequent royal processions of Kings Jeongjong and Taejong, but stalled after Taejong's death when such processions became rare. Renewed need from ordinary travelers eventually prompted work to resume in 1475, and the bridge was completed in 1483 under King Seongjong. Its flat, level surface — said to feel like walking on open ground — earned it the nickname 'Jebangyo.' It's the largest bridge built in early Joseon, resting on 64 stone piers shaped like diamonds to reduce water resistance. Heavy flooding in Seoul in the 1920s washed away part of the bridge, and it was rebuilt in the 1970s, though a concrete section added during that restoration means it has somewhat lost its original appearance.

서울-신당동-박정희-가옥-2764329.name: Park Chung-hee House, Sindang-dong, Seoul
서울-신당동-박정희-가옥-2764329.description: This is the house where former President Park Chung-hee lived with his family from 1958 until moving to the official residence of the Supreme Council for National Reconstruction in Jangchung-dong in 1961 (128.93㎡). The only surviving house from a 1930s housing development built by the Joseon Urban Development Company in Sindang-dong, it's recognized as an important record of Korean residential history and designated National Registered Cultural Heritage No. 412. Restored based on family photographs and press materials from when the family lived here, it has been open to the public since 2015.

자매공원-331506.name: Sister City Park
자매공원-331506.description: Sister City Park was built in May 1977 to mark the sister-city agreement between Seoul and Ankara, Turkey, themed around Turkish culture. The park's Ankara House, a two-story building styled after a traditional Ankara vineyard house, was built in 1992 and opened as a folk museum in 1995. Inside, a traditional Turkish living space has been recreated, displaying around 800 folk items including Ottoman-era traditional dress and handicrafts — a prayer room, living room, and kitchen on the first floor, and a parlor, guest room, and bedroom on the second, offering a look at Turkish domestic life. Benches scattered throughout the park are a popular rest spot for nearby office workers.

대림동-차이나타운-2402981.name: Daerim-dong Chinatown
대림동-차이나타운-2402981.description: Daerim-dong Chinatown grew up in the early 2000s as ethnic Korean-Chinese residents settled around Daerim Station, forming a residential-style Chinatown quite different from the traditional port-based Chinatowns of Incheon or Busan — this one is woven tightly into everyday neighborhood life. About 40% of the shops in Daerim Central Market are run by Korean-Chinese residents, and nearby are banks, lodgings, and restaurants catering to the community. The market serves everything from traditional Chinese dishes like mala tang and hot pot to fusion fare, along with street food fragrant with Chinese ingredients and spices.

오금공원-754063.name: Ogeum Park
오금공원-754063.description: Ogeum Park, in Ogeum-dong, Songpa-gu, sits diagonally across from the Songpa Police Station near Garak-dong, close to Ogeum Station (Line 5). Built eco-consciously into a 200m-elevation hill, it offers a pleasant natural setting of trees, flowers, and lawns. Its nature-study garden, home to around 30 species of wild flowering plants and 20 native shrub species, lets visitors observe a variety of plants while strolling. With 5 plazas and 9 walking-trail routes plus a children's playground, it draws a steady stream of local residents. Sports facilities — a sports ground, tennis courts, a pool, badminton courts, a gateball court, a fitness area, and an inline hockey rink — serve as fitness and leisure space for residents and students.

서울-양천고성지-127216.name: Yangcheon Fortress Site, Seoul
서울-양천고성지-127216.description: Yangcheon Fortress Site is a mountaintop fortress on Gungsan, in Gaya-dong, Gangseo-gu, built to enclose the main ridge and upper branch ridges of the peak. Gungsan sits where Anyangcheon Stream meets the Han River, making it a key defensive point guarding the lower Han River. The fortress has a steep north face toward the Han River and a gentler south slope, running about 220m and covering 29,370㎡. Old records document the fortress, and traces of the wall — foundation stones and building blocks — can still be seen. Tradition holds that General Gwon Yul stationed his forces here during the Japanese invasions of the 1590s before crossing the Han River to his victory at Haengju Fortress; together with Haengju Fortress and Odusanseong, it was a key defensive point for the lower Han River.

경성-부민관-폭탄-의거지-2373204.name: Site of the Gyeongseong Bumingwan Bombing
경성-부민관-폭탄-의거지-2373204.description: This is where a bomb was set off to disrupt a pro-Japanese rally at Gyeongseong Bumingwan on July 24, 1945. Built in December 1935, Gyeongseong Bumingwan was the city-run theater of colonial-era Seoul — equipped, unusually for its time, with heating, cooling, lighting, and sound systems — used both for theater performances and for pro-Japanese wartime mobilization rallies. In May 1945, young activists in their early twenties, led by Jo Mun-gi, formed the Korean Patriotic Youth Party, watching for a chance to strike against Japanese rule. When word spread that a pro-Japanese rally led by collaborator Park Chun-geum would be held at Bumingwan on the evening of July 24, 1945, the group secretly planned to bomb the venue, obtaining dynamite from a nearby construction site and planting two homemade bombs near the restrooms at the back of the hall the night before. The bombs went off around 9pm, shortly after Park Chun-geum took the stage, bringing the rally to an abrupt halt. Coming less than a month before liberation, the Bumingwan bombing was a powerful demonstration of an unbroken national will for independence. The site is now occupied by the Seoul Metropolitan Council building, with a marker stone noting the bombing.

3-1독립운동기념탑-1825460.name: March 1st Independence Movement Monument
3-1독립운동기념탑-1825460.description: Built with contributions gathered from across the nation, this monument stands in Namsan Park, Jangchung-dong, Jung-gu, to carry forward the noble spirit of the March 1st Movement — the struggle for national independence from Japanese colonial rule — and to cultivate a broad sense of patriotic devotion. Construction began on August 15, 1998, the 50th anniversary of the founding of the Republic of Korea, and was completed on March 1, 1999, the 80th anniversary of the March 1st Movement. The tower stands 19 meters and 19 centimeters tall, a deliberate reference to the movement's year, 1919. The March 1st Movement was the world's first large-scale nonviolent independence movement and the first joint movement uniting Cheondogyo, Christian, and Buddhist believers, becoming a touchstone for nonviolent movements worldwide, including China's May Fourth Movement and India's non-cooperation movement. It's 920m from Exit 6 of Dongguk University Station (Line 3).

순정효황후윤씨친가-1606014.name: Family Home of Empress Sunjeonghyo (Consort Yun)
순정효황후윤씨친가-1606014.description: This house shows the full character of a top-tier Joseon aristocratic residence. It's a reconstruction modeled on the Ok-in-dong Yun family house within Namsangol Hanok Village, relocated in 1996 when Namsangol Park was developed from its original site in Jongno-gu. Said to have been the residence of Empress Yun at the end of the Joseon dynasty, the house has an overall square floor plan with the main gate facing east. The men's quarters, positioned at the southeast corner of the lot overlooking the whole neighborhood, are built in a raised pavilion style. The women's quarters' main hardwood-floor hall spans six bays facing east, with all column capitals using the simplest bracket style and an unusual cloud-shaped support bearing the horizontal beams. The men's quarters' roof has hipped-and-gabled eaves at all four corners, its gable ends finished in brick. On the kitchen's gable wall, small vented windows above the servants' quarters roof allow natural ventilation, finely carved, with the column corners and crossbeam joinery all finely detailed.

우남-이승만박사-동상-1829744.name: Statue of Dr. Syngman Rhee (Unam)
우남-이승만박사-동상-1829744.description: This statue of Dr. Syngman Rhee (pen name Unam), on the grounds of Baejae High School, honors his contributions to the independence movement. Built in 1984, it stands 3m tall and 1m wide. Rhee, who studied Chinese classics from a young age, enrolled at Baejae Hakdang (predecessor of today's Baejae High School, where the statue now stands) and studied modern subjects there, going on to lead reform efforts in the enlightenment-era press and the Independence Club before being imprisoned. After his release, he traveled to the U.S., earned a doctorate, and worked abroad on diplomacy, national education, and public outreach for Korea's liberation. Following liberation and the founding of the Republic of Korea's government in 1948, he served as its first president.

민영환-자결터-605961.name: Site of Min Yeong-hwan's Self-Sacrifice
민영환-자결터-605961.description: This is where Min Yeong-hwan took his own life in protest of the Eulsa Treaty. A loyal official of late Joseon, Min had argued for the treaty's annulment in front of the palace, but after Japanese military police forcibly dispersed the protest, he took his own life at 6am on November 30, 1905, leaving behind three farewell letters addressed to the people, to foreign diplomats, and to the emperor. After his death, his bloodstained clothes and sword were hung in a room; when the room was reopened the following May, four bamboo stalks were said to have grown up through the floorboards and the bloodied clothing. People took this as his loyalty manifesting as 'blood bamboo,' and called the plant 'jeoljuk' ('bamboo of integrity'). At the site of his death, in front of the Hana Building in Insa-dong, Jongno-gu, stands a memorial sculpture depicting the bamboo said to symbolize his loyalty alongside a lattice door, and displaying the dagger and farewell letters used in his self-sacrifice.

탑골공원-팔각정-1605933.name: Tapgol Park Octagonal Pavilion
탑골공원-팔각정-1605933.description: This pavilion in Tapgol Park, Jongno 2-ga, was designated a Seoul Tangible Cultural Property in 1989. It was built in 1897 (King Gojong's 34th year) alongside Tapgol Park itself, at the suggestion of the British financial advisor J. McLeavy Brown. Tapgol Park was Korea's first modern-style park, and the octagonal pavilion is believed to have been built as a performance venue for the military band during the grand 1902 celebrations marking the 40th anniversary of Gojong's enthronement. It was originally used by the imperial court orchestra, performing publicly only on Sundays; as crowds grew eager to hear the music, it opened to the public on weekdays too starting July 1913. The building has an octagonal floor plan with an octagonal, layered-eave roof and a five-tiered stone platform base. Its fine proportions later served as a model for Namsan's octagonal pavilion. During the March 1st Movement of 1919, students and citizens gathered in front of this pavilion to read the Declaration of Independence aloud and march through the streets shouting for Korean independence.

해공신익희선생동상-1836300.name: Statue of Sin Ik-hui (Haegong)
해공신익희선생동상-1836300.description: Gangdong-gu built this statue in Cheonho-dong to honor independence activist Sin Ik-hui (pen name Haegong), who devoted his life to Korea's independence and the development of its democracy. Born in Gwangju, Gyeonggi-do, in 1894, Sin entered Waseda University in Japan in 1912, where he organized the overseas students' unifying body Hakwoehoe and published its journal Hakjigwang to promote national spirit and independence. Returning home in 1913, he opened a study institute to spread new culture, and in 1919 distributed the Declaration of Independence and led demonstrations. Fleeing arrest, he escaped to Shanghai and joined the founding of the Provisional Government, serving as deputy interior minister, cabinet secretary-general, acting foreign minister, and interior minister before returning home at liberation. He later served as the Democratic Party's chief officer and National Assembly speaker, and as the party's 1956 presidential candidate campaigned tirelessly for democracy until he died of a cerebral hemorrhage aboard a campaign train.

몽마르뜨공원-753981.name: Montmartre Park
몽마르뜨공원-753981.description: Montmartre Park sits above Seorae Village. Because many French residents live in the surrounding neighborhood, the park was named after Paris's Montmartre. True to its name, it's filled with art and romance — though modest in size, it's dotted with French poetry and sculptural artwork, including bust sculptures of major French artists like Vincent van Gogh, Paul Gauguin, and Pablo Picasso. It also has a memorial garden dedicated to the beloved Korean singer Lee Mi-ja, plus a playground, making it a nice spot for a family picnic. At the far end of the park is the Nue Bridge, connecting to Seoripul Neighborhood Park — cross it to continue a walk through Seoripul Park, where different flowers bloom with the seasons.

광나루한강공원-250252.name: Gwangnaru Hangang Park
광나루한강공원-250252.description: Between Gangdong Bridge and Jamsil Railway Bridge, Gwangnaru Hangang Park preserves the Han River's natural character better than almost anywhere else — its sandbars and large reed beds formed naturally from sediment carried down from upstream. As Seoul's only protected water-source area, boating and water sports are banned here, keeping the water clean and clear; the greenery of Achasan to the north and the roughly 2km of riverside reed beds together make for a beautiful landscape. Gwangnaru Hangang Park is also a habitat for migratory birds. Nearby are numerous heritage sites, including the Amsa-dong prehistoric settlement, making this a place where nature and culture come together well.

우이동만남의광장-3065955.name: Uidong Meeting Plaza
우이동만남의광장-3065955.description: Uidong Meeting Plaza is a walking park with a valley, set at the foot of Bukhansan. With a playground and walking trails, it has a nearby dulle-gil loop trail and valley that make it a good spot for a family visit. It's home to Bonghwanggak, a training center for Cheondogyo leaders built by movement leader Son Byeong-hui, who led the March 1st Movement, and a Korean War memorial honoring 88 fallen soldiers from Gangbuk-gu. It also offers fine views of Bukhansan's Wangwanbong Peak nearby, and connects to the Bukhansan Dulle-gil trail. A small cafe at the entrance serves tea and coffee. There's no dedicated parking, and it's about 500m from Exit 2 of Bukhansan Ui Station.

광나루자전거공원-3065938.name: Gwangnaru Bicycle Park
광나루자전거공원-3065938.description: Gwangnaru Bicycle Park, in Gangdong-gu, is a cycling path connected to Gwangnaru Hangang Park. Riders can pedal along the Han River and take in the surrounding parks on the way. Its biggest draw is riding while taking in the Han River's night view and sunset. Bikes can be rented, and a nearby tire-pump station also makes it easy for those bringing their own bike. A children's cycling-education area and bike track make it good for families and couples to ride together at a relaxed pace. The entrance is about 900m from Exit 3 of Amsa Station.

서울-영휘원-순헌황귀비-과-숭인원-이진-126527.name: Yeonghwiwon (Tomb of Imperial Consort Sunheon) and Sunginwon (Tomb of Yi Jin), Seoul
서울-영휘원-순헌황귀비-과-숭인원-이진-126527.description: Yeonghwiwon is the tomb of Imperial Consort Sunheon (Lady Eom), a consort of Emperor Gojong of the Korean Empire; Sunginwon is the tomb of Grand-Prince Yi Jin, the first son of the last Crown Prince, Uimin. Consort Sunheon (1854–1911) entered the palace at age 8 and became a court lady serving Empress Myeongseong, later becoming a royal consort of Gojong after giving birth to Prince Yeongchin in 1897. Elevated to imperial consort in 1903, she was a committed advocate for women's modern education — founding Jinmyeong Girls' School and Sookmyung Girls' School, and donating roughly 2 million pyeong of land and personal funds to Yangjeong School when it faced financial trouble. Following Japan's forced annexation, she died in 1911 at Deoksugung. Grand-Prince Yi Jin (1921–1922), first son of Crown Prince Uimin and Crown Princess Yi, was born in Japan, briefly returned to Korea the following year, and died suddenly at Deoksugung the day before returning to Japan; Emperor Sunjong ordered an elaborate funeral and had the tomb built at its present site. Yeonghwiwon was built according to Joseon-era conventions for a royal consort's tomb, with a red-spiked gate, a ritual pavilion, and a stele hall, and stone guard-figures ringing the mound; Sunginwon was built similarly but with smaller stone furnishings and a smaller mound.

반공-청년운동-순국-열사-기념비-2373326.name: Memorial to the Martyrs of the Anti-Communist Youth Movement
반공-청년운동-순국-열사-기념비-2373326.description: The Anti-Communist Youth Movement Memorial Committee erected this monument on October 9, 1968, in Yejang-dong, Jung-gu, to honor the souls of patriots who died fighting in the anti-communist youth movement and to carry forward their spirit of national devotion. The inscription reads: 'This monument is not stone — it is the heart of anti-communist fighters.' It stands as a tribute to young patriots, many with much of their lives still ahead of them, who gave their short lives for their eternal homeland. Namsan's octagonal pavilion and its beacon-fire station are nearby, making it easy to visit together.

청량사-서울-482126.name: Cheongnyangsa Temple (Seoul)
청량사-서울-482126.description: Cheongnyangsa is a training ground for Buddhist nuns on the southern slope of Cheonjangsan — the famous 'Dolkkoji Seungbang,' long known as one of Korea's four great nunneries. Cheongnyangsa and Dolkkoji Seungbang were originally separate temples, but after Empress Myeongseong was assassinated in 1895 and her tomb was later built on Cheongnyangsa's original site, the temple moved to its present location, merging around the same time with the declining Dolkkoji Seungbang. In late Joseon it was a popular retreat for city residents, and during the colonial era it drew many patriots and eminent monks — independence and Buddhist reform leader Han Yong-un (Manhae) reportedly stayed here for a time, with his 60th-birthday celebration quietly held here in 1939. Being set in a residential area, Cheongnyangsa runs a daycare center and has a playground for children. Its oldest building, Geungnakbojeon, has a small pagoda-like finial at the center of its roof, and — likely because of the sloped site — the buildings are arranged in a tight, almost split-level layout. Small but complete, the temple has a Gwaneumjeon, Muryangsujeon, Daeungjeon, guest hall, meditation hall, and quiet-practice hall.

경찰혼-1826438.name: Police Spirit Memorial
경찰혼-1826438.description: In 2006, this memorial was built in Dangsan-dong, Yeongdeungpo-gu, to honor local police who fell in the line of duty during the chaotic postwar period after liberation, the Korean War, and its aftermath. Yeongdeungpo Police Station erected the monument to carry forward the patriotism and sacrifice of its fallen officers and to console their families. Before and during the Korean War, Yeongdeungpo police stood against the North Korean invasion for the safety and peace of the people and fell in operations against communist guerrillas; even after the war, officers continued to give their lives working year-round to secure public safety for local residents. Yeongdeungpo Police Station holds a memorial ceremony for them every year. (Source: Ministry of Patriots and Veterans Affairs website)

관악도시농업공원-3428259.name: Gwanak Urban Farming Park
관악도시농업공원-3428259.description: This urban farming park in Gwanak-gu gives city residents a chance to experience agriculture, connect with nature, and try out a more sustainable way of living. Designed with a range of facilities and programs to bring farming activities into the city itself, it has become a hands-on educational space and 'ring' for residents to make their own.

안국사-3450146.name: Anguksa Shrine
안국사-3450146.description: Anguksa enshrines a portrait of the great Goryeo-dynasty general Gang Gam-chan. Naksungdae, nearby, is known as General Gang's birthplace, and the shrine takes its name, 'Anguk' ('peace for the nation'), from his pen name.

구로거리공원-3447964.name: Guro-geori Neighborhood Park
구로거리공원-3447964.description: A space for local residents' rest and leisure that brings together Guro-gu's urban character and its natural surroundings. The park regularly hosts local festivals, performances, and exhibitions, with these cultural events helping to strengthen bonds within the community.

연의근린공원-2611679.name: Yeonui Neighborhood Park
연의근린공원-2611679.description: Yeonui Neighborhood Park is Korea's only park built around an ecological retention basin, using a patented Ministry of Environment bio-filtration technology for ecological water purification. It has deck paths and an ochre-clay path, wildflowers planted on its slopes, and four fountains that put on a night-lit display for residents out exercising after dark. Along the walking path, an ecological-experience program teaches visitors about the park's plants and insects in a simple, engaging way. The park is also home to Eco Space Yeonui, a facility combining exhibition, education, and healing spaces — an exhibition hall on the first floor, an education space on the second, and a rooftop garden on the third. Eco Space Yeonui runs a family ecology program every weekend, with a different theme each month.

대현문화공원-3456362.name: Daehyeon Culture Park
대현문화공원-3456362.description: Daehyeon Culture Park, in Daehyeon-dong, Seodaemun-gu, gives local residents access to nature and leisure space, and is a beloved retreat amid the surrounding city. It has well-landscaped walking paths and green space, plus exercise equipment and rest areas supporting residents' health and leisure. As a neighborhood park, it's especially well known as a familiar, frequently visited local spot.

디큐브시티-해바라기-공원-3448217.name: D-Cube City Sunflower Park
디큐브시티-해바라기-공원-3448217.description: Connected directly to Sindorim Station, D-Cube City Sunflower Park is an easily reached pocket of nature and rest in the city. Covering about 6,000 pyeong, it has a sunflower plaza, a wildflower valley, a rose tunnel, and a 770-seat outdoor theater among its facilities. At night, its dazzling lights and fountain make it especially popular with families, friends, and couples.

장충단공원-126491.name: Jangchungdan Park
장충단공원-126491.description: Jangchungdan Park is a national memorial park carrying the patriotic spirit of the anti-Japanese resistance. Set on Namsan's northeastern slope, the site once held a garrison defending the southern approach to the city walls during King Yeongjo's reign. After Empress Myeongseong was assassinated by Japanese agents at Gyeongbokgung in 1895, Emperor Gojong built the shrine Jangchungdan in 1900 to console the spirits of officials and soldiers who died defending her, holding memorial rites there each spring and autumn through 1908. The shrine burned down during the Korean War, and only its monument survived, relocated to the current site in 1969. In 1919, Japan built a temple and a park on the site to erase Korean national identity — all removed after liberation. Designated a neighborhood park in 1984, Jangchungdan Park was absorbed into the broader Namsan Park natural-park system, though the remaining section still carries the old name. The area holds several heritage sites — the Jangchungdan monument, Supyo Bridge, Seungjeongjeon Hall, Gwanseongmyo and Waryongmyo shrines — plus the March 1st Movement Monument, the Monument to the Korean Confucian Scholars' Petition to Paris, a poetry stone for Manhae Han Yong-un, and statues of Yu Gwan-sun, Yi Jun, and Kim Yong-hwan.

문화철도959-2592089.name: Culture Railway 959
문화철도959-2592089.description: Culture Railway 959, run by the Guro Culture Foundation, is a multi-purpose cultural space on the 3rd floor of Sindorim's elevated Line 1 station building. Built to activate unused space and boost the local economy, it's a joint project of Guro-gu, the Guro Culture Foundation, and the artist collective Toka Art. It hosts the 959 Art Platform, where 15 young artists create work, an art gallery exhibition space, and quarterly culture classes offering hands-on arts-and-culture programs, alongside spaces for events and gatherings run by local residents, groups, and clubs together with the resident young artists.

창천근린공원-3456475.name: Changcheon Neighborhood Park
창천근린공원-3456475.description: Changcheon Neighborhood Park, in Changcheon-dong, Seodaemun-gu, is a green space built for local residents' rest and leisure. Its trees and lawns make it a pleasant setting for a walk or picnic, with a walking path, benches, and exercise equipment offering both health and leisure to residents. It's especially well suited to family visits, with play facilities for children and exercise space for adults, making it a place for different generations to connect and relax together. Near Barampark Children's Park, it's a convenient neighborhood park for the Sinchon area, with different scenery through the seasons — flowers in full bloom in spring, vivid foliage in autumn.

사가정공원-1117141.name: Sagajeong Park
사가정공원-1117141.description: Sagajeong Park opened in April 2005 at the entrance to the Myeonmok mineral-spring district in Myeonmok-dong. It's named after Seo Geo-jeong (pen name Sagajeong), an early-Joseon literary figure who once lived near Yongmasan. Four of his best-known poems are inscribed on poetry stones throughout the park, letting visitors enjoy classic verse as they stroll. With a picnic area, children's playground, fitness facilities, a naturalized stream, the Sagajeong traditional pavilion, a multi-purpose plaza, and streamside rest areas, it offers residents a high-quality, pleasant place to relax and has become a signature spot in Jungnang-gu.

서울숲-곤충식물원-3442142.name: Seoul Forest Insect & Plant Garden
서울숲-곤충식물원-3442142.description: Seoul Forest Insect & Plant Garden is a nature-study space inside Seoul Forest Park where visitors can observe tropical plants and a variety of insects. With a themed botanical garden, a specimen exhibition room, and a butterfly ecology hall, it offers an educational, enjoyable experience for families. Admission is free, and it's open Tuesday through Sunday.

서울성북-미디어문화마루-2773558.name: Seoul Seongbuk Media Culture Maru
서울성북-미디어문화마루-2773558.description: Seoul Seongbuk Media Culture Maru is a multi-purpose cultural facility built by the city and Seongbuk-gu to bring a library, performance hall, pool, and other cultural amenities to northeastern Seoul, an area historically underserved by basic infrastructure — and, reflecting the growing importance of media, to serve as a media hub offering media education and startup support. Spanning 9,484㎡ across 2 basement and 4 above-ground floors, it has a community sports facility (Mulbit Pool) in the basement, a public library (Geulbit Library) and the Seoul Viewers' Media Center on the 1st–3rd floors, and a roughly 320-seat performance hall (Kkumbit Theater) on the 4th floor. It's a 5-minute walk from Exit 1 of Gireum Station (Line 4).

연화사-서울-337508.name: Yeonhwasa Temple (Seoul)
연화사-서울-337508.description: Yeonhwasa, on the slopes of Cheonjangsan in Hoegi-dong, Dongdaemun-gu, is a branch temple directly administered by the Jogye Order. Hoegi-dong takes its name from Hoereung, the tomb of deposed Consort Yun, mother of King Yeonsangun, once located here; a small temple built as her memorial temple now occupies the site. Named Yeonhwasa ('lotus flower temple') for the idea that all sentient beings share the nature of a pure lotus blooming from the mud, it was built by Yeonsangun as a place to pray for his mother's soul and to guide her wrongly-taken spirit to rest. Today, Hoereung has been relocated to Seosamneung, and a girls' school now occupies the original site, so little of the old landscape remains, but the small temple beneath it carries the lineage forward, still holding Buddhist paintings commissioned by many court ladies as memorial offerings for Consort Yun and Queen Seonui.

봉원사-서울-126503.name: Bongwonsa Temple (Seoul)
봉원사-서울-126503.description: A thousand-year-old traditional temple, Bongwonsa was registered as a traditional temple in 2011, and its Amitabha banner painting and bronze bell were designated Seoul Tangible Cultural Heritage in July 2014. Regular dharma gatherings are held by its lay Buddhist groups — the Avalokiteshvara Society, Hwaeom Society, choir, and folk-painting society — and it hosts affiliated institutions including the Yeongsanjae Preservation Society, the Yeongsanjae Training Center, the Korea Yeongsanjae Preservation Association, and Okcheon Beomeum College, which trains practitioners in Buddhist ritual chant. Set in the middle of the city, Bongwonsa works to promote and pass on Yeongsanjae, a traditional Buddhist ritual, both domestically and abroad, upholding its standing as a leading center of traditional Buddhism while striving to be a place where faith can deepen in everyday life.

삼룡사-2774468.name: Samryongsa Temple
삼룡사-2774468.description: Samryongsa, on the slopes of Yongmasan in Jungnang-gu, belongs to the Cheontae Order of Korean Buddhism and serves around 3,000 practicing Buddhists. It retains the beauty of a traditional temple even in the middle of the city. Spanning one basement and four above-ground floors, the 4th floor holds the Daebulbojeon main hall, the 3rd floor the Lotus Sutra meditation hall, the 2nd floor a smaller worship hall and rest space for lay groups, and the 1st floor administrative offices, a dining hall, and kitchen. Active lay groups include a choir, a youth association, a tea-ceremony society, a Pure Land practice group, a flower-arranging society, and a volunteer group. The temple blends a range of Buddhist events and cultural activities and maintains close ties with the surrounding community.

북한산-족두리봉-2779558.name: Bukhansan Jokduri-bong Peak
북한산-족두리봉-2779558.description: Bukhansan, the guardian mountain of Seoul, spans Eunpyeong-gu, Seongbuk-gu, Gangbuk-gu, and Dobong-gu as well as Uijeongbu, Yangju, and Goyang in Gyeonggi-do. Its dramatic ridgeline — running from the highest peak, Baegundae, to Insubong in the east and Mangyeongdae in the south — draws hikers year-round. Jokduri-bong, at 370m, is the southwesternmost peak of Bukhansan. Seen from a distance, its shape resembles a jokduri, a traditional Korean bride's headpiece, which gave the peak its name; it's also called Surisan for its resemblance to an eagle's head, and 'Little Insubong' for how closely it echoes the shape of Insubong itself. From Bulgwang Station, it's about a 50-minute climb to the peak — short, but moderately challenging, with steep stairs and some exposed rocky sections that call for caution.

서울-삼전도비-231897.name: Samjeondo Monument, Seoul
서울-삼전도비-231897.description: This monument, erected at the demand of Qing Emperor Hong Taiji after Joseon's defeat in the Manchu invasion, records his achievements as part of the humiliating peace treaty Joseon was forced to sign. Erected in 1639 (King Injo's 17th year), it stands 3.95m tall and 1.4m wide, titled 'Monument to the Virtue and Achievement of the Great Qing Emperor.' The Jurchen people, who had long paid tribute to Joseon, grew rapidly as Ming China weakened, founding the Later Jin and then Qing dynasties and increasingly pressuring Joseon — relations deteriorated sharply once the renamed Qing demanded Joseon submit as a vassal. In 1636, Qing's Hong Taiji personally led 100,000 troops into Joseon, launching the Manchu invasion. King Injo, having held out at Namhansanseong Fortress, ultimately surrendered at the Samjeondo ferry crossing on the Han River, signing the humiliating peace treaty. After the war, Qing forced Joseon to erect this monument honoring the emperor's achievements. The front bears Mongolian script on the left and Manchu script on the right, with Chinese characters on the back — making it an important source for research on Manchu and Mongolian language. (Source: Songpa-gu Office website)

남산인권숲-3447859.name: Namsan Human Rights Forest
남산인권숲-3447859.description: Namsan Human Rights Forest occupies the former site of the Korean Central Intelligence Agency. Only the site remains today, now returned to forest, with a monument and information panels symbolizing democracy. It's more than a rest space — it doubles as a place for reflection and education.

남산순환나들길-2783557.name: Namsan Circular Trail
남산순환나들길-2783557.description: Rising in the heart of the city, Namsan is a Seoul landmark and a year-round retreat loved by residents. The Namsan Dulle-gil trail circles the mountain from N Seoul Tower, a pleasant 7.3km walk taking about 2.5 hours, linking a Northern Circular Path suited to everyone, a History & Culture Path lined with stories, a Nature Ecology Path and Wildflower Path showcasing Namsan's natural setting, and a Forest Path. The Northern Circular Path, in particular, was designated a barrier-free trail — wheelchair users, stroller users, and visually impaired visitors can navigate it without much help from a companion. Running 3.4km from the Namsan cable car entrance to the National Theater, it bans cars and bicycles for a safe walk; braille blocks run down the center of the path, with the convention that sighted walkers keep to the right out of consideration for others — earning it the nickname 'the path of consideration.' Highlights along the trail include the Ahn Jung-geun Memorial Hall, the 'Photo Island' photo zone at Jamdubong (named for its resemblance to a silkworm's head), the 'Locks of Love' at the N Seoul Tower plaza, and N Seoul Tower itself, a broadcast and observation tower near the summit overlooking the city.

원통사-서울-346995.name: Wontongsa Temple (Seoul)
원통사-서울-346995.description: Wontongsa, on Dobongsan in Dobong-gu, is a branch temple directly under Jogyesa, head temple of the Jogye Order's 1st district. Flanked by Suraksan and Samgaksan and facing the Han River, it has long been known as a training site set at one of Dobongsan's most auspicious spots. Great monks from the early-Joseon Muhak Daesa to the modern-era Mangong, Dongsan, and Chunseong all achieved great enlightenment while staying here, and it's also famous as a place of prayer to Avalokiteshvara. During King Yeongjo's reign, high officials discussed matters of state and cultivated their minds here, making it a well-known spot among the era's Confucian scholars. The grounds today hold a stone grotto said to be where Joseon founder Yi Seong-gye once prayed, and a large rock below the Yaksajeon hall bears an inscription said to have been carved after Taejo dreamed of becoming a heavenly minister on the day he finished praying. A rock behind the temple known as Ui-am is said to resemble Avalokiteshvara praying toward the Buddha, and was originally called 'Gwaneum-bong' — nearby rocks shaped like a tiger, an elephant, and a crane all seem to bow toward it, which may be why people consider this a naturally blessed sacred site of Avalokiteshvara.

도봉서원-서울-1955511.name: Dobong Seowon (Confucian Academy), Seoul
도봉서원-서울-1955511.description: Dobong Seowon, dedicated to Jo Gwang-jo and Song Si-yeol, two of the most important Neo-Confucian scholars of early and late Joseon, was a royally chartered academy and is today the most representative Confucian academy site remaining in Seoul, where renowned poets and scholars including Yi Hang-bok (Baeksa) left writings. Though most of its structures were lost when the 1871 order abolishing Confucian academies had it torn down, unlike other academy sites in Seoul, the foundation of its shrine and a cluster of rock inscriptions documented as part of the historic academy remain largely intact in the valley in front of the site, making its boundaries relatively easy to trace. The site has also long been celebrated in literature and poetry as a scenic spot, giving it further value worth preserving. (Source: Korea Heritage Service)

종묘광장공원-126492.name: Jongmyo Plaza Park
종묘광장공원-126492.description: Jongmyo is the shrine housing the memorial tablets of Joseon's kings and queens, including those posthumously honored. Its buildings were recognized for their cultural and architectural value and registered as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in December 1995. Within the park, a well once used by Joseon kings visiting Jongmyo has been rebuilt, along with a statue of independence figure Yi Sang-jae and a green space with amenities. Covering 39,669㎡ in front of Jongmyo, with parking facilities, Jongmyo Plaza Park is widely used by Seoul residents as a place to relax.

국립중앙박물관-전통염료식물원-1604580.name: National Museum of Korea Traditional Dye Plant Garden
국립중앙박물관-전통염료식물원-1604580.description: This garden, in the National Museum of Korea's rear grounds, revives the value of Korea's traditional dye culture. The museum planted and maintains the traditional dye plants Korean ancestors once used to create color, both to preserve traditional dyeing culture and to enrich visitors' everyday lives. Carefully researched dye plants and ornamental trees are planted together here, making it an educational spot introducing visitors to the plants used in traditional dyeing. It offers a chance to understand Korean tradition through connection with nature and to appreciate the beauty of dye plants, deepening understanding of the history and process of dyeing. In spring, its plum blossoms bloom in full, making it a well-known hidden photo spot.

서울-약현성당-250330.name: Yakhyeon Cathedral, Seoul
서울-약현성당-250330.description: Yakhyeon Cathedral is a small-scale church building. As the number of Catholics grew after religious freedom was granted in 1886, it was established as a mission chapel under Myeongdong Cathedral. In 1891, Father Doucet, then parish priest of Myeongdong Cathedral, secured land in Hapdong, and Father Coste, the vicar-bishop, designed and oversaw construction, completing Yakhyeon Cathedral the following year, 1892. The area was once used for growing medicinal herbs, giving it the name 'Yakjeonhyeon' ('hill of medicinal fields'), later shortened to 'Yakhyeon.' Notably, this is Korea's first Western-style church building. Though it shows some Gothic elements, its rounded, heavy arched roof and narrow window openings give it an overall Romanesque brick character. Relatively small, its side windows sit at a low eave height with round rather than pointed arches, while the front entrance and the projecting side entrances each form pointed arches with a more distinctly Gothic look.

서울학도병참전기념비-1829573.name: Seoul Student Soldiers War Memorial
서울학도병참전기념비-1829573.description: When Korean forces retook Seoul on September 28, 1950, and pushed north, they gathered student volunteers who had signed up to serve as artillerymen at Yongsan High School. Of the many students who applied, 341 were selected, departing Seoul on October 20 and arriving in Pyongyang the next day, assigned to the 18th Artillery Battalion of the 17th Division. They went on to serve at the front, some earning officer commissions, until the armistice on July 23, 1953; 112 of them were killed or went missing. The Fallen Student Soldiers' Tower was built at Yongsan High School in 1956 to honor the 80 Yongsan High students who served as artillerymen and the many other classmates who served in other units, all giving their youth for their country. The Seoul Student Soldiers War Memorial was erected by the Seoul Student Artillery Veterans Association in 2005, the 55th anniversary of their service, and a memorial plaque listing all 341 names was added on the 65th anniversary in 2015. Every June and October, the veterans association, Yongsan High School, and its alumni association jointly hold a ceremony honoring their patriotism.

노량진컵밥거리-3067187.name: Noryangjin Cup-Bap Street
노량진컵밥거리-3067187.description: Noryangjin Cup-Bap Street is a cluster of food carts serving cup-bap, a Noryangjin specialty. Cup-bap is a street food developed by the carts lining the study-academy district of Noryangjin in Dongjak-gu, created with budget-conscious exam-prep students in mind. Originally called 'pocha-bap' ('food-cart rice'), the term 'cup-bap' came into wide use around 2011. It's a one-bowl meal of stir-fried kimchi rice topped with a choice of egg, sausage, ham, tuna, and other toppings, typically priced between 4,000 and 5,000 won, with toppings chosen to taste. In 2018, Dongjak-gu installed information signage for visitors and later added rest spots between the carts. Beyond cup-bap, the carts also sell bunsik (Korean snack food), rice noodles, corn dogs, and waffles, letting visitors sample a range of street food while strolling.

갈산공원-1116925.name: Galsan Park
갈산공원-1116925.description: Unlike most of Yangcheon-gu's other rounded hills, Galsan boasts a striking cliff-like drop on its eastern side, carved into a blade-like ridge by the long erosion of Anyangcheon Stream — giving it the original name 'Kalsan' ('knife mountain'), later softened to 'Galsan.' A children's traffic-safety park sits at the entrance, a central plaza and walking paths offer rest halfway up, and an observatory at the summit gives a sweeping view of Yangcheon. Alongside the Galsanjeong pavilion at the summit stands Korea's first triangulation survey point.

장수공원-열녀문-2611601.name: Jangsu Park (Yeollyeomun Gate)
장수공원-열녀문-2611601.description: One of Sinwol-dong's landmarks, Jangsu Park stretches from the 'Street with Flowing Water' at Sinjeong Negeori intersection to the covered road in Sinwol-dong, with reflexology paths, badminton courts, and other facilities for both walking and exercise. The Haenuri Fountain Plaza on the Street with Flowing Water is a beloved children's play spot doubling as a cooling summer retreat. Jangsu Park's central plaza also holds a memorial plaque honoring veterans who fought in the Korean War and the Vietnam War. Walking along the park's trail leads to a Yeollyeomun ('gate of the virtuous woman') monument, honoring a woman of the Jeonui Yi clan who, widowed young, stopped eating out of grief for her husband and died in her late twenties. When the court learned of this, it issued a commemorative plaque in 1729 honoring her devotion.

아차산-어울림정원-742972.name: Achasan Harmony Garden
아차산-어울림정원-742972.description: Achasan Eco Park, showing significant wear after more than 20 years, was renovated and reopened in May 2023 as Achasan Harmony Garden, built around six themes: wind, roses, fragrance, roof-tile ends, stone, and sound. It includes a Wind Garden planted with ornamental grasses that ripple in the breeze; a Rose Garden showcasing roses, a symbol of love and beauty; a Fragrance Garden of scented trees offering a quiet rest amid gentle aromas; a Wadang Garden, its stone wall inspired by Goguryeo-era roof-tile ends excavated at a nearby fortress, filled with colorful flowers; a Stone Garden blending stone, trees, and flowers; and a Sound Garden for savoring flowing water and other natural sounds. Pergolas, rest decks, sun loungers, and lighting round out the garden.

g밸리-4차산업체험관-2990289.name: G Valley 4th Industrial Revolution Experience Center
g밸리-4차산업체험관-2990289.description: Partnering with top companies across various fields, the G Valley 4th Industrial Revolution Experience Center runs a range of hands-on programs letting visitors experience the fast-changing technologies of the 4th industrial revolution firsthand. Its curriculum covers the basics of drones, coding, VR, and 3D printing, moving from foundational practice and simulations to real-world application. Bringing four representative technologies together in one space lets participants deepen their understanding through both individual and cross-disciplinary experiences, and gain insight into applying these technologies across different fields.

강서역사문화거리-3043735.name: Gangseo History & Culture Street
강서역사문화거리-3043735.description: Gangseo History & Culture Street runs through the Gaya-dong area, home to a scattering of historical and cultural sites, transforming a once-neglected streetscape into one rich with history and culture. The Gungsan area of Gaya-dong was the administrative center of Yangcheon County in the Joseon dynasty, leaving behind many heritage sites throughout the neighborhood. A landmark sculpture marks the start of the street out Exit 1 of Yangcheon Hyanggyo Station (Line 9); pillar-shaped information panels along the way introduce each site and its location. The street links the Gyeomjae Jeong Seon Art Museum, Gungsan Tunnel, Soakru Pavilion, the Yangcheon Fortress Site, and Yangcheon Hyanggyo (Confucian school) — about an hour's walk at an easy pace. After dark, the street transforms with beautiful lighting, a chain of illuminated sculptures quite different from its daytime look.

서울퓨처랩-3036898.name: Seoul Future Lab
서울퓨처랩-3036898.description: Seoul Future Lab is a digital playground built on 'funology' (fun + technology) that makes the 4th industrial revolution easy and fun to experience, open to everyone from preschoolers to adults, with immersive, story-based programs exploring future technology. It's organized into four zones: a Metaverse Experience Hall, an Innovation Technology Hall, an AI Convergence Hall, and a Creative Education Hall. The Metaverse Hall offers an immersive virtual-space experience to build understanding of future tech; the Innovation Technology Hall lets visitors playfully learn about robotics and autonomous driving through games; and the AI Convergence Hall offers an AI-and-robotics-based escape-room game and generative-AI 3D image creation. Each hall runs a variety of programs — XR career experiences, UAM races, a 'Robolympics,' digital twins, AI robot challenges, and AI creation workshops — though the schedule varies by day, so it's worth checking before visiting.

송파구자원순환공원-2761745.name: Songpa Resource Circulation Park
송파구자원순환공원-2761745.description: Covering 40,024.87㎡ across 5 buildings in Jangji-dong, Songpa-gu, this themed park combines a modern waste-management facility with public park space. Handling recyclables, food waste, and both bulky and general household waste from the Jangji-dong area, it uses advanced processing systems and has been developed as an eco-friendly themed park running a range of hands-on programs for residents. Its Resource Circulation Exhibition Hall has permanent hands-on exhibits highlighting the importance of resource circulation and environmental conservation.

호국무공수훈자공적비-1837037.name: Monument to Decorated War Veterans
호국무공수훈자공적비-1837037.description: Erected in 2010, the 60th anniversary of the Korean War, through the joint effort of Seongdong-gu and its chapter of the Decorated Veterans Association, this monument honors the achievements and noble patriotic spirit of veterans decorated for valor defending the nation in the Korean War and fighting for world peace in the Vietnam War. Set atop a circular pedestal with steps, it consists of three towers: the first bearing the monument's inscription, the second listing the names of all 279 decorated veterans, and the third with a dedication text and supporting organizations. It measures 6.8m by 6.8m and stands 5m tall.

우면산-소망탑-2779508.name: Umyeonsan Somang-tap (Wishing Tower)
우면산-소망탑-2779508.description: Umyeonsan, straddling the border between Seocho-gu, Seoul, and Gwacheon, Gyeonggi-do, gets its name from its resemblance to a sleeping cow. Easily reached from the city center, it draws hikers from dawn until late at night. Its gentle grade means hiking boots aren't really necessary, making it a favorite with beginners — most adults can reach the summit, where the Somang-tap wishing tower stands, in just over an hour. The tower itself grew stone by stone as visitors began stacking rocks here, each carrying a personal wish, eventually forming today's large cairn. The nearby observation deck offers a view striking enough to be named one of Korea's outstanding scenic viewpoints, with a night view that ranks among the finest in the city. The mountain also holds several historical sites, including a prehistoric dolmen and the Baekje-era temple Daeseongsa.

송재서재필선생상-1829610.name: Statue of Seo Jae-pil (Songjae)
송재서재필선생상-1829610.description: This statue in Seodaemun Independence Park honors Seo Jae-pil, an enlightenment and independence activist from Boseong, South Jeolla. Songjae Seo Jae-pil launched Korea's first private newspaper, The Independent, on April 7, 1896. With the cooperation of Yun Chi-ho, Yi Sang-jae, and others, he founded the Independence Club, tore down Yeongeunmun Gate — a symbol of subservience to China — and, with public donations, built Dongnimmun (Independence Gate) on the site as a symbol of Korean independence, converting the old Mohwagwan reception hall into Dongnimgwan for the club's meetings and offices. Through public debates, he rallied citizens to discuss national independence and reform, organized the People's Joint Association, and helped block Russia's attempt to lease Jeolyeongdo Island in Busan — greatly advancing the public's sense of independence and civil rights. After the March 1st Movement of 1919, he headed the Korean Commission to America and Europe set up by the Provisional Government in Washington, devoting his entire fortune to the cause, before passing away in the United States on January 5, 1951, at age 87.

이대거리-2667611.name: Ewha Womans University Street
이대거리-2667611.description: This alley runs from the main gate of Ewha Womans University to Sinchon train station. Once plagued by vacancies as the fashion industry slumped, the street revived after 2017 as sharp, style-conscious shops run by young entrepreneurs began moving in. Take-out cafes and small eateries line its alleyways, and true to its fashion-hub reputation, it's packed with distinctive clothing stores, hair salons, cosmetics shops, shoe stores, accessory boutiques, and nail salons. (Source: Seodaemun-gu Office website)

연남동끝자락길-2784040.name: Yeonnam-dong Kkeutjarak-gil
연남동끝자락길-2784040.description: True to its name ('the edge of Yeonnam-dong'), this street sits at the far end of the neighborhood and was once known as an escape route during wartime. Young people drawn to the warmth of this neighborhood's tangle of narrow alleys came together to create Yeonnam-dong Kkeutjarak-gil. The street is filled with distinctive shops that take pride in their own individual brand — cafes, tea houses, dessert shops, and restaurants each with their own personality, making it a fun place to wander and browse.

헬로애니멀-2763818.name: Hello Animal
헬로애니멀-2763818.description: Hello Animal is an indoor zoo along the Jungnangcheon Stream near Bangak Station (Line 1) in Dobong-gu, Seoul. It's home to around 50 species of small animals, including cute little reptiles and birds, with professional keepers on hand to explain each animal — visitors can get up close, touch and interact with them, and even feed and observe them directly. There's underground parking in the building, and the Dobong-gu Office parking lot is also available on weekends.

독산-근린공원-2756142.name: Doksan Neighborhood Park
독산-근린공원-2756142.description: This small neighborhood park in Doksan 1-dong, Geumcheon-gu, has a walking trail and exercise facilities, and sits right across the street from Anyangcheon Stream, making it easy to combine a visit to both. At its center, a large artificial-turf soccer field (16,528㎡, built in 2017) ringed by dense trees is popular with soccer clubs — after reserved booking hours, it opens to local residents, letting children play safely too. Beyond the soccer field, it has a gateball court, five badminton courts, and a walking trail and exercise facilities along the Anyangcheon riverside.

쌈지-어린이공원-2756153.name: Ssamji Children's Park
쌈지-어린이공원-2756153.description: Ssamji Children's Park, also known as Sangsang ('Imagination') Park, is a 982㎡ children-only park tucked into a residential neighborhood in Doksan 4-dong, Geumcheon-gu. From small attachments on the slide to a large rock-climbing wall beside the stairs, it's a space where kids can build strength and coordination through play, with a variety of differently sized and shaped slides, jumping areas, and energy-generating exercise bikes among its play equipment.

국제음식문화거리-international-food-street-25918.name: International Food Street
국제음식문화거리-international-food-street-25918.description: International Food Street sits in an area with heavy foot traffic — Sindorim Station, a large shopping mall, and a restaurant district all nearby draw an estimated 20,000-plus visitors a day. It's also home to the UNESCO Asia-Pacific education institute, which welcomes around 15,000 trainees a year. Selling food from a range of countries, it's a fun spot for sampling different cuisines, and regularly hosts cultural festivals, flea markets, and other events.

구로리어린이공원-2733981.name: Guro-ri Children's Park
구로리어린이공원-2733981.description: Guro-ri Park is a children's park in Guro-dong, Guro-gu, Seoul, reimagined from a once-plain, aging children's park into a space that nurtures creativity, with a range of facilities and landscaping designed for children. It operates as a children-only park, restricted to children and their guardians.

긴고랑공원-2756575.name: Gingorang Park
긴고랑공원-2756575.description: This neighborhood park near Achasan in Gwangjin-gu is made up of several walking routes, including the Gingorang-gil trail and Jumong Bridge. Part of the Achasan Ansim Dulle-gil (safe loop trail), it's well used by both local residents and hikers. Walking the mural-lined Gingorang-gil trail through the hillside Junggok-dong neighborhood, where the Achasan and Yongmasan valley paths meet, leads to the mountain's entrance; information panels along the way make it easy to navigate. Motorcycles and bicycles are banned throughout the park. It's about a 17-minute walk from Exit 1 of Achasan Station (Line 5) to near the Junggok 4-dong community center, or about 18 minutes from Exit 4 of Gunja Station (Line 5).

윤극영가옥-2777943.name: Yun Geuk-yeong House
윤극영가옥-2777943.description: The city of Seoul designates and manages notable modern and contemporary cultural heritage worth passing on to future generations as 'Seoul Future Heritage,' including sites like the National April 19th Cemetery. The Yun Geuk-yeong House holds special significance as the very first site selected. Active in the 1920s–30s, Yun Geuk-yeong composed beloved children's songs including 'Half Moon,' 'New Year's Day,' 'Three Umbrellas in a Row,' and 'Icicle.' He's also known as 'Grandfather Half Moon' for producing Korea's first collection of children's songs, 'Half Moon.' The house where he once lived now serves as the Half Moon Cultural Center, welcoming visitors. The space displaying his personal effects has taken on the warmth of age, feeling almost like visiting a grandfather's home, and the gentle sound of children's songs playing softly brings back memories of childhood.

빨래골-2773346.name: Ppallaegol (Laundry Valley)
빨래골-2773346.description: Ppallaegol is a neighborhood in Suyu-dong, Gangbuk-gu, named for the abundant, clear water in the eastern valley of Samgaksan once used as a laundry spot and gathering place — the name literally means 'laundry valley.' It sits in the valley of the Kalbawi Ridge, where Bukhansan stretches down toward the city. Deeper in the valley is a hermitage called Samseongam, and on the hillside to the left is the grave of Gongcho Yim Sang-sun, marked by an unusually shaped tombstone. The 'Old Village Ppallaegol Festival,' held since 2016, keeps the name in active use today. From Exit 3 of Suyu Station (Line 4), take bus 03 to the Ppallaegol terminal stop, then walk about 200m further in.

마루공원-2752525.name: Maru Park
마루공원-2752525.description: Maru Park, in Ilwon-dong, Gangnam-gu, has parking and is a good spot for a walk with a dog. On nice days, many visitors set up tents and chairs under the park's shade structures. It has two play areas — one a standard playground with slides and swings, the other lined with various road traffic signs, combining traffic-safety education with a space to 'ride' trains and cars; the cushioned playground surface keeps kids safe even if they fall.

강남-264570.name: Gangnam
강남-264570.description: The area around Gangnam Station is the transit hub of the Gangnam district. Teheran-ro runs east from Gangnam-daero toward Jamsil, while the western direction connects toward Sadang; from the Kyobo Tower intersection, the road links to the Express Bus Terminal, connecting to Noryangjin and western Seoul, and north via Hannam Bridge to Gangbuk, and south via Yangjae to new towns like Bundang and Seongnam in the greater capital region. Gangnam Station draws huge crowds largely because it's such a convenient meeting spot — well suited to gatherings, events, and personal meetups alike. Weekday evenings and weekend afternoons regularly see crowds around Exits 10 and 11 and in front of the Lotte Cinema. Convenient transit and a wealth of fashion stores, theaters, and large bookstores draw shoppers even from distant parts of the city. Gangnam-gu also runs the Gangnam Medical Tour Center, a hands-on tourism hub offering both general visitor services and a look at two of the district's strengths — medical care and Korean pop culture. Aimed at foreign medical tourists, it offers hospital referrals, interpretation, tax-free shopping help, airport pickup, sightseeing information, and hotel booking, alongside general travel brochures, a rest area, and free luggage storage.

이상의집-3044977.name: Yi Sang's House
이상의집-3044977.description: This is the site of the house where Yi Sang (born Kim Hae-gyeong, 1910–1937), a leading figure of Korean literary modernism, lived from age three for over 20 years. Facing demolition, the site was purchased in 2009 by the National Trust of Korea Cultural Heritage through public fundraising and corporate sponsorship, and has been preserved and managed since. It was originally part of his uncle's roughly 300-pyeong estate, later subdivided into 10 lots built up with hanok houses; the Trust purchased part of the original site. Inside, a bust and portrait of Yi Sang stand alongside an archive of his work arranged chronologically along one wall. To the left, a heavy concrete door frame and large black steel door open onto a stairway rising through a dark, windowless space to the roof; at the top, opening the door to the outside floods the space with bright light — a widely praised symbolic design, expressing through architecture the yearning for freedom amid a dark era and difficult personal circumstances.

와룡공원-1019041.name: Waryong Park
와룡공원-1019041.description: Waryong Park connects with Samcheong Neighborhood Park, Changgyeong Neighborhood Park, and the Bugaksan Urban Nature Park. Its shallow soil once made it hard for trees to grow, and the forest here was largely acacia — but residents' participation in a 'ten million trees for life' planting campaign has transformed it into a park with lush greenery and seasonal blooms. In spring especially, cornelian cherry, plum blossoms, azaleas, and forsythia bloom throughout, making it a great destination for a family outing.

훈련원공원-1605966.name: Hullyeonwon Park
훈련원공원-1605966.description: This site once held the Hullyeonwon, the training academy responsible for soldiers' martial-arts training and battle-formation instruction. Established in 1392 (Joseon founder Taejo's 1st year) as the Hullyeon-gwan, it was moved here under King Taejong, where a training hall was built south of the main office for archery and other martial-arts practice and the military examination; it was renamed Hullyeonwon in 1466 (King Sejo's 12th year). Before today's Hullyeonwon Park and parking lot were built, the site held a wooden building decorated with red brick, its interior framed with red pine felled on Baekdusan and floated down the Yalu River to the Yellow Sea. When that building was demolished, some of its recovered timber was used to make the park's information panel, preserving a trace of its old character. Opened June 30, 1997, it has a lawn, drinking fountain, misting fountain, and other landscaping, along with a management office, restrooms, and benches.

이탈리아-의무부대-6-25전쟁-참전기념비-1835206.name: Italian Medical Corps Korean War Memorial
이탈리아-의무부대-6-25전쟁-참전기념비-1835206.description: Although Italy was not a UN member during the Korean War, it responded to an appeal from the International Red Cross Federation, dispatching a 67-member medical unit on October 16, 1951, stationing a field hospital at Seoul Usin Elementary School. The Italian medical unit treated not only wounded soldiers but civilians too, caring for about 230,000 people, military and civilian alike, until January 30, 1955, with particular focus on eradicating parasites among the civilian population; during the Yeongdeungpo train accident of September 17, 1952, its rapid response minimized casualties. On June 2, 1989, the Italian Ambassador to Korea installed a memorial plaque on the wall of Seoul Usin Elementary School, the unit's former base, to honor their noble service; when the building was demolished in July 1999, the plaque was relocated to its present site with support from Korea's Ministry of Patriots and Veterans Affairs, on August 10, 1999.

생명보험교육문화센터-2455084.name: Life Insurance Education & Culture Center
생명보험교육문화센터-2455084.description: The Life Insurance Education & Culture Center is Korea's first life-insurance experience hall, with an exhibition hall, digital experience zone, and hands-on learning center that make financial and insurance concepts — often intimidating for kids — easy and fun to understand. Its programs range from hands-on learning open to everyone from elementary schoolers to adults, to career-focused sessions for middle and high schoolers. The hands-on program uses tablets for self-directed learning: visitors start in the exhibition hall with displays on the history of life insurance and its social contributions, then use VR and AR to learn the principles of financial insurance, before working through 13 hands-on missions in the experience hall covering what money is, how insurance developed and works, and why social insurance matters — testing their own spending habits and playing games simulating life-stage risk management, with a team quiz battle at the end to review. The career program covers financial insurance basics and the range of careers in the field. Beyond Seoul, there's also a branch in Busan, and all programs are free.

크라운해태-키즈뮤지엄-2451912.name: Crown Haitai Kids Museum
크라운해태-키즈뮤지엄-2451912.description: Run by the confectionery group Crown Haitai, this children's experience space helps parents and kids learn creativity and critical thinking together through play, building cooperation and communication skills along the way. Its Imagination Playground exhibition space has 8 distinct zones, each with its own themed activity, where children build artistic sense, physical coordination, communication, social skills, and imagination through self-directed play. Its Kinetic Art zone lets kids admire a moving sculpture before rolling balls down their own tracks; the Media Play Zone reacts to children's movements with floor-projected video; the Block Playground lets kids build their own creations and narrate the story behind them; and the Cloud Imagination Playground uses a wall-projected cloud-and-sky village to spark imagination. The Wind Science Lab lets kids feel air movement through paper fluttering in a wind tunnel, the Climbing Zone offers hands-on physical play on a climbing wall, the Free Drawing Zone lets kids draw wherever they like, and the Science Art Zone uses light balls to build sensory development and integrated thinking.

여의도공원-문화의마당-2774305.name: Yeouido Park Culture Plaza
여의도공원-문화의마당-2774305.description: Yeouido Park opened in 1971 on the site of a former airstrip as Yeouido Plaza, becoming a hub for national events and public leisure. In January 1999, its black asphalt was removed and it reopened as a green retreat, now organized into four zones: a Nature Ecology Forest, a Culture Plaza, a Lawn Plaza, and a Traditional Korean Forest. The Culture Plaza hosts festivals, performances, and other public cultural events. Within the plaza stands a flagpole and an Air Force memorial sculpture — an airplane — giving the space added meaning. That aircraft is a C-47 transport plane, which landed at Yeouido on August 18, 1945, carrying the Korean Liberation Army's advance unit alongside the U.S. OSS — meaning Korean forces reached Seoul just three days after liberation. The C-47 exhibit stands at the very spot where the plane touched down.

양천생활안전체험교육관-2611575.name: Yangcheon Life Safety Experience Center
양천생활안전체험교육관-2611575.description: Located beside the Yangcheon Culture Center, the Yangcheon Life Safety Experience Center opened on August 25, 2016. Yangcheon-gu built the space to help prevent everyday safety accidents and build residents' emergency-response skills through hands-on training, fitting a compact but thorough facility into part of an existing parking lot. The 264㎡ center's CPR training room and life-safety experience area let visitors practice chest-compression CPR, using an automated external defibrillator, fire extinguishing, and smoke evacuation.

양천구어린이교통안전교육장-1105980.name: Yangcheon-gu Children's Traffic Safety Education Center
양천구어린이교통안전교육장-1105980.description: Inside Galsan Park, this center teaches children how to prevent traffic accidents through hands-on training based on common real-world accident scenarios, including how to properly cross at traffic lights and crosswalks in a realistically built training ground. It draws many kindergarten and elementary-school visitors and serves as a living classroom. Safety-education bookings can be made through the Korea Safety Federation's website; sessions run three times a day, combining classroom instruction with hands-on practice.

아시아공원-1603175.name: Asia Park
아시아공원-1603175.description: Asia Park was built in 1986 alongside the athletes' and press village apartment complexes ahead of the 1986 Asian Games, close to the Seoul Sports Complex and other competition venues. Its broad green space, filled with pine and jujube trees and a variety of flowers, includes a nature-and-light sculpture, an outdoor performance stage, a Poetry and Painting Plaza, the Songpa Arts Center, and a monument to Buri Island — widely used as cultural and leisure space for local residents. The Arts Center plans and runs local cultural programs to build community pride and unity, expanding residents' access to culture through festivals and educational lectures. (Source: Parks of Seoul)

한양공원-2758809.name: Hanyang Park
한양공원-2758809.description: Hanyang Park, in Songpa 2-dong, Songpa-gu, is a long, narrow park running alongside the Songpa Hanyang Apartments 2nd complex, offering nearby residents a rest space it has maintained for over 30 years. Modest in size — a small park by neighborhood-park standards — it has all the essentials: a walking path, benches, a fountain, and exercise facilities, plus a combined children's play structure for safe play. The park is home to a wide variety of trees, including junipers not commonly found in other parks.

마천공원-2757653.name: Macheon Park
마천공원-2757653.description: Macheon Park, in Macheon-dong, Songpa-gu, sits within a residential neighborhood. Though modest in size, it's well equipped with a management office, restrooms, a children's playground, and walking paths. Centered on its sports ground and playground, the park's paved paths are good for a walking workout, and the tree-lined slope to the side makes for a scenic stroll. Its sports ground, laid with artificial turf, is fairly large; a senior citizens' center sits to one side, with exercise equipment out front. Macheon Park provides rest and fitness for both children and adults in the neighborhood.

서울-고려대학교-본관-252527.name: Korea University Main Hall, Seoul
서울-고려대학교-본관-252527.description: This main hall of Korea University's predecessor, Boseong College, was commissioned by Kim Seong-su, who managed the school at the time; construction began in 1933 and finished in 1934, designed by Park Dong-jin. Three stories tall (six at its central tower), it's built primarily of granite in a symmetrical Gothic style, with an H-shaped floor plan and a spacious central hall. The two stone pillars at the entrance are carved with tiger statues symbolizing the school's spirit, and the pillars at the central rear entrance are carved with mugunghwa (rose of Sharon) blossoms. At the time of construction, its lavish, imposing interior and exterior were unmatched by any other school building in the country. (Source: Korea Heritage Service)

백련사-서대문-128028.name: Baengnyeonsa Temple (Seodaemun)
백련사-서대문-128028.description: This thousand-year-old temple, on the slopes of Baengnyeonsan in Seodaemun, was founded in 747 (Silla's King Gyeongdeok's 6th year) by the monk Jinpyo Yulsa, originally named Jeongtosa. It was renamed Baengnyeonsa in the first year of King Jeongjong's reign; Jeongjong, Joseon's 2nd king, stayed here to recuperate after ceding the throne to his brother Taejong. Legend holds that Princess Uisuk, daughter of King Sejo, widowed at 20, wandered here in her grief and found deeper meaning in life — the temple was then designated her memorial temple and renamed Baengnyeonsa ('white lotus temple'). Another account holds that a white lotus suddenly bloomed in its pond one summer, prompting the name change from its earlier name, Jeongtosa. Destroyed during the Japanese invasions under King Seonjo, it was quickly rebuilt and has been renovated many times since. The temple today includes the Geungnakjeon hall (completed 1965), the Muryangsujeon hall housing an Amitabha Buddha, the Wontongjeon hall housing an Avalokiteshvara, plus a Yaksajeon, Gwaneumjeon, Myeongbujeon, Samseonggak, Dokseonggak, and bell pavilion.

고촌이종근기념관-2453179.name: Gochon Lee Jong-geun Memorial Hall
고촌이종근기념관-2453179.description: The Gochon Lee Jong-geun Memorial Hall is a founding exhibition hall for Chong Kun Dang, honoring the philosophy and achievements of its founder, Chairman Lee Jong-geun (pen name Gochon), and preserving his spirit of fearless entrepreneurship, modest living, and generosity toward those in need. It's also a pharmaceutical-history museum covering both Korean and international medical history. It has two galleries: the first traces Lee Jong-geun's life, Chong Kun Dang's growth, and the broader history of medicine in Korea and abroad; the second is a hands-on experience hall letting visitors engage directly with the spirit of challenge and generosity Lee embodied.

정몽주-동상-127308.name: Statue of Jeong Mong-ju
정몽주-동상-127308.description: This statue, erected in October 1970, stands in the green space near the entrance to Yanghwa Bridge in Hapjeong-dong. Jeong Mong-ju (pen name Poeun, 1337–1392), a late-Goryeo scholar-official, topped the state examination in 1360 and served as head of the Office of Special Advisers. Skilled in diplomacy with Ming China and Japan, he also achieved notable success suppressing Japanese pirate raids and Jurchen incursions, while establishing relief granaries to aid the poor, spreading Confucian learning, and mastering Neo-Confucian philosophy. He worked to rationalize social ethics and morality, remaining loyal to Goryeo even as the dynasty's fortunes waned and a new political force rose to challenge it — a loyalty that ultimately cost him his life. Many of his poems survive, including his famous loyalty poem 'Dansimga,' and he excelled at calligraphy and painting as well. Remembered as one of the 'Three Recluses of Goryeo' for his unwavering loyalty, he was posthumously honored as chief state councilor in 1401 and enshrined in the Confucian shrine under King Jungjong.

마포전차종점-3-1운동-만세-시위지-2373247.name: Site of the March 1st Movement Rally at Mapo Tram Terminal
마포전차종점-3-1운동-만세-시위지-2373247.description: The Mapo tram terminal once stood where the approach to Mapo Bridge meets Mapo Station on Seoul Subway Line 5 today — the endpoint of the tram line that ran through central Seoul from the colonial era until the late 1960s. This site holds historical significance as the location of a March 1st Movement rally where about 1,000 people gathered around 8pm on March 1, 1919, to demonstrate for independence. That day, after the Declaration of Independence was proclaimed at Taehwagwan and read aloud at Tapgol Park's octagonal pavilion around 2pm, thousands of students marched through the streets shouting for Korean independence, moving from Jongno through Gwanggyo, City Hall, and Namdaemun before converging here at the Mapo tram terminal around 8pm as the sun set; demonstrations continued near Yonhui College until around 11pm without a single incident of violence — a wholly peaceful, nonviolent expression of the Korean people's will for independence. A monument and heritage marker remain at the site today, drawing visitors who come to reflect on this chapter of history.

노들나루공원-2763685.name: Nodeul Naru Park
노들나루공원-2763685.description: Nodeul Naru Park, in Noryangjin, Dongjak-gu, was formerly known as Noryangjin Reservoir Park before being renamed. It has a ground-level fountain, an outdoor stage, and various exercise facilities, along with green lawns, a rose plaza, and several walking routes.
